subtopic: MR. CAMERON (NANAIMO)    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF SPEECH BY MINISTER OF FINANCE
MR. CAMERON (NANAIMO)    REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF SPEECH BY MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. I have in my hand a report from the Toronto Telegram of Saturday, April 16, 1955 which I should like to place on the record. It is headed "Trotskyites among M.P.'s says Harris", and reads in part as follows:
There are Trotskyites among the C.C.F. members of parliament at Ottawa, finance minister Walter Harris told Liberals attending the annual meeting of the Toronto-York Liberal Association at the King Edward today.
He said expulsion of Toronto members of the C.C.F. party charged with being Trotskyites should not be taken as an unusual happening. He suggested some C.C.F. M.P.'s might be expelled on similar grounds.
The finance minister called his recent budget "a plain, ordinary Liberal budget", not "a fantasy of imagination or a stand-pat budget".
From consulting Hansard, Mr. Speaker, I understand that the minister has denied the accuracy of this report and of course, without hesitation, I accept his assurance on that score. Nevertheless, I cannot refrain from expressing my regret that he did not take advantage of the first opportunity he had to correct this false statement. When he was approached, I am told, by the man who reported the meeting, immediately following the meeting, and asked if he would care to elaborate on his statement that there were Trotskyites among the C.C.F. group, I think it is regrettable that the minister failed to take advantage of that opportunity to deny this false report and that for nearly 48 hours he permitted it to wend its slanderous trail back and forth across this country. I may say that I find it rather curious. I have been in public life for many years longer than has the Minister of Finance. For over 20 years, sir, I have spoken in public on every controversial question that has come before the country. My speeches have been widely reported. I have yet to be misquoted. It appears to be an occupational disease of Liberal cabinet ministers.
In the house yesterday, when challenged on this statement, the Minister of Finance 50433-186J
took occasion to read extracts from a letter which I had written on behalf of a man called Stanton who was later expelled from the Ontario section of the party to which 1 belong, on a charge of being a Trotskyite. It is perfectly true that I wrote that letter on behalf of Paddy Stanton. I wrote it because I had known him for many years on the Pacific coast. I have in mind one particular occasion that I am going to call to the attention of the house because I think it will explain why I wrote such a letter.
The occasion to which I refer was one during the 1945 federal election campaign in the city of Prince Rupert when a gang of communist thugs attempted to break up my meeting. At that time, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that they were supporting the Liberal party, their leaders having been released on the unfortunate Canadian electorate by the Liberal government of that day for their own purposes. When this gang of communist thugs attempted to break up my meeting, this man Paddy Stanton, fool that he was, attempted to settle the matter with his fists.
It was such things that I had in mind when I acceded to his request that I would speak on his behalf before the Ontario convention of the C.C.F. or write on his behalf, as I was obliged to do. If, as it now appears, Paddy Stanton has, since the time I knew him on the Pacific coast, become a Trotskyite, and if, on account of that fact, he has to some extent betrayed my trust and delivered me to my enemies, I am still not sorry that I wrote that letter because, when you reach my time of life, you realize that such things as requital of past favours, loyalty, decency and honesty are more important than are even the most glittering political prizes. I want to say this now categorically, Mr. Speaker. I am not nor have I ever been a Trotskyite; I am not nor have I ever been a Trotskyite sympathizer; and anyone who states that I am is an unmitigated liar.
The C.C.F. is the only political party to which I have ever belonged. The democratic socialist principles of that party are the only political principles I have ever endorsed or supported. I want to say this. If anyone, by a combination of statements outside this chamber and references within this chamber, should ever impute to me the charge of being a Trotskyite or a Trotskyist sympathizer he

Inquiries of the Ministry would not only be an unmitigated liar but he would be an unprincipled scoundrel and a contemptible coward.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce. maintopic: REPORTED REDUCTION IN CANADA'S SHARE OF WORLD MARKET
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his question and also for sending me a copy of the Wheat Review. Possibly I might say a word in reply to this question. As the hon. gentleman knows, and as the house knows, a note
Inquiries of the Ministry was sent to the United States government on this question and that note was tabled in this house. There has been no written reply from the United States government to that note, though we have been pressing for such a reply almost daily and have expressed to the United States government, through the state department, our anxiety to get it without delay. We have had an expression of regret from the authorities in Washington that they have not yet completed their reply.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 5, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is two weeks today since budget day. The tumult and the shouting have pretty well died down, and I think people have had a chance to see what the budget really does amount to. I feel that in a sense it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. I hope the minister enjoyed the applause while it lasted. It must be very pleasant to be acclaimed as the little friend-I was going to say of all the world, but I do not mean that. I mean a very fractional amount of the world, namely those who were benefited by the budget. Everyone's heart seems to respond instinctively to tax reductions; but it is only as people have looked further and have found the real situation that they have realized how thin it all is.
They are gradually realizing another thing, too, and that is that the origin of it is unsound, namely that it is borrowed. It does not come because the government has been

making savings. It comes because the government has borrowed money, and thus laid a greater burden on the backs of the taxpayers.
I think that the first joy and enthusiasm of the married man with two children and $2,500 a year must have been chilled a great deal when he found that, so far as this year is concerned, he would have four cents a week more to take home to his family. Well, there will not be much excitement over that.
And so far as the corporation taxes are concerned, the reduction from 49 per cent to 47 per cent is of course a move in the right direction; but it is only a trifling move. And neither shareholders nor consumers can hope to get much benefit from it.
But the thing that puzzles me and continues to puzzle me about this budget is that I cannot understand it. I cannot understand the minister's reasoning. The minister certainly puzzled me very much by the speech he made in Montreal last November; but during the last two weeks he has puzzled me still more, because it seemed to me that he gave reasons for doing one thing, and then did exactly the opposite.
I wish to support that by quoting from what the minister said. These were his words;
I am sure that all will agree that when employment and incomes are high and the economy expanding at a normally healthy rate, we should fully balance our budget with a modest amount for the reduction of debt.
I think everyone will agree with that. He then went on-and I call attention of hon. members closely to this:
Conversely when the rate of economic advance slackens and the economy as a whole is not fully employed, a moderate budgetary deficit should be no cause for alarm.
I call the attention of hon. members to that phrase "when the rate of economic advance slackens". Now, the minister spent some considerable time in underlining the fact that the economy was not slackening, but that it was quickening. His whole budget was based upon a big pickup, a pickup that seems extravagant. His whole argument was that the economy was quickening and not slackening. Therefore, having said that, how could he turn around, with a quickening economy- a very substantial quickening, with almost extravagant hopes-and nevertheless indulge in this deficit.
The only reason I can give-and while the minister denies it and I shall read his denial in a moment-the only reason I can give is that in spite of the fact that he did not like to mention the unpleasant word, he really did this because of the hope that he might in some way help unemployment. He did not 50433-187
19, 1955	2945
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell say that, because it was not down his alley to say that things were not good. His whole line was to say that things were good.
According to the Canadian Press he said, in an interview after the budget, that "he had not cut personal income taxes and sliced 2 per cent off corporation taxes to stimulate the economy, indicating he did not feel the economy necessarily needed stimulating". That is quoted from the Canadian Press.
Now, taking the minister's speech, and subsequent interviews, as I say the matter to me is a complete puzzle. It is inevitable I think to assume that the cuts were made, among other reasons, to help unemployment by stimulating the economy. But the minister denies that. He says that he just felt "taxes were too high." Of course they were too high. But there is a proper way to reduce taxes, and there is an improper way. And he took the improper way, rather than the proper one. The proper way is to reduce expenditure. But of course that sort of thing is not dreamed of in the philosophy of this government.
There is another way; but I repeat he reduced taxes because he felt they were too high. In other words, it was a popularity measure. According to the minister's own statement, his only reason for doing so was to please the people. It was just a popularity measure.
Now, is it possible that he felt that, if he gave any other reason for it than his desire to please the taxpayer, he would lose their gratitude because they might feel it was not being done for them? However that may be, we have this curious situation, what someone has called an ambidextrous budget. Certainly I felt that the right hand did not know what the left hand was doing. I was glad to find this statement made by a responsible journalist, because it expressed my feeling and gave me further justification for my own belief.
I wondered if something was wrong. I have often wondered if there was something wrong with my head, and I wondered if there was something wrong with me, that I could not understand. But when I found that many other people held the same views as I do I came to the conclusion that my views were justified.
However much kindness there was in the minister's great heart when he reduced taxes, we cannot ignore the fact that a deficit has results. Whether he knew that or not, a deficit has results. And we cannot get away from that fact. One of those results is to provide some stimulus, a very tiny stimulus, but some stimulus, by increasing purchasing

But apparently the minister cannot lace admitting that, because to admit that the economy needed a shot in the arm was all against what he had said earlier-that there was a substantial pickup. I am glad to say it looks as if there was; but you cannot have it both ways.
No serious person can ignore the fact that there are fiscal, financial implications; and we taxpayers who carry the load are entitled to ask the minister some questions. Let me set out here an imaginary conversation between the minister and a reasonably intelligent taxpayer.
The taxpayer asks: How much money did you take last year?
The minister: About $4,107 million.

The taxpayer:	That means that you
borrowed $194 million which we shall have to repay.

He left me puzzled in Montreal last November, and I have been puzzled ever since, and the speech which he made two weeks ago did not take away that puzzlement; it really added to it.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, if the relief had come from government economies how differently we would have felt. We would have felt that perhaps at long last the spending spree was over. We would have hoped that some of the economies that we have been so generously suggesting all these years could be made. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that this budget divides the Canadian taxpayers into two groups. First of all, there are the beneficiaries, but secondly there are the people who are not beneficiaries but who are going to pay. Everybody is going to pay. Not everybody gets a handout but everybody is going to pay, and the people who are less well off and who get nothing are going to pay for the relief of the others. That strikes me as an odd idea. I do not know whether the minister thought of that; I was rather pleased when I thought of it. Maybe it was thought of; maybe they just decided to let the poor people tough it out. They have had it tough enough, anyway; perhaps they can tough it out further.

Let me recapitulate. The minister says that in an expanding economy we should have a surplus, and then he tells us that the economy is expanding. He says further that in a slackening economy we may have a deficit. But as I have pointed out already, he has made it clear that the economy is not slackening, and, ignoring his own reasoning so far as I am able to follow it, ignoring the clear reasoning he has given us, he then plunges into a deficit. I shall have something more to say about that.
You cannot face both ways forever. You may be able to do it on budget night and get away with it, but it catches up with you.

The press is catching up. It is interesting to note that a loyal, stouthearted supporter of the government-I think I am describing them correctly-the Toronto Star, ignores the minister's exhilaration and evidently feels, indeed it calls, the outlook uncertain. It is apparently not filled with optimism as the minister is, but it has a good deal of hesitation and doubt, and it says this:
Mr. Harris' maiden speech will come as a disappointment to the many Canadians who hoped it would stimulate production and reduce unemployment.
You see, the Star is apparently bold enough to believe that everything is not quite perfect and would like to see the economy stimulated. It is not like the minister. He does not want to stimulate it. It does not need stimulation, but the Star apparently thinks it does. I continue to read from the Star:
Taken as a whole it is really an unimaginative stand-pat budget that in itself will provide little relief from our present economic problems.
You see, the Star is not convinced; it does not regard it as a simple reduction in taxation; it does not think that it is nothing but vote-catching, whatever others think. Whether the minister thinks it or not, whether the minister admits it or not, it has other results as well. As a matter of fact, the Star pays the minister the compliment of taking him seriously and it says, if things are really in a bad way-and I feel there is something in this-if things are in as bad a way as the Star thinks they are, then there might be an argument for their suggestion of a much larger deficit, though I do not agree with it. Nevertheless, if the minister started out with the view of the situation that the Star has he 50433-18"i
19, 1955
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell might quite probably have reached their conclusion. However, the minister can comfort himself with the Free Press of Winnipeg. They really have come through in grand style. I remember very well reading this because I have a great respect for the Free Press, when they are right, and I think this was right. I read this with great respect last December. The Free Press said:
The fiscal discipline of balancing the budget cannot be abandoned. To urge anything of the kind is the very depth of Conservative irresponsibility.
That was said in December, and now we are in April, Mr. Speaker. The Free Press swallows the dose. It troubles them a bit. They are not too enthusiastic about the budget. They have little postern gates left open where they can get through later on if it turns out to be not a great success; but nevertheless, by and large, the Free Press gives it a kind of qualified blessing. They think it is not a bad budget. As a matter of fact, they do a little twisting and squirming and they make themselves believe it is not a deficit budget at all. I do not know how you can do it. It is in some kind of higher synthesis that I have not been able to reach.
The Star's words of course underline a very important question of fiscal policy which ought to be most seriously considered, particularly from the point of view of two groups in the community: first of all, all those on fixed incomes who cannot protect themselves against rising costs; and secondly, and perhaps at the present moment particularly, the agricultural community who are squeezed between the upper and nether millstones. Their costs are certainly not going down. I am afraid there is every reason to believe that it will require an effort to keep their prices where they are now.
If we are going to be serious people we must face the fact that there is no doubt whatever about the tendency of a deficit. The tendency of a deficit, indeed the actual effect of a deficit, is to create additional purchasing power through borrowed money. The minister cannot play fast and loose with hundreds of millions of dollars and say that it is going to have no effect on anything. Something is going to happen. Deficits mean higher purchasing power with a tendency toward higher prices.
The minister will say, in fact the governor of the Bank of Canada said the other day, that the tendency will be for unemployment to offset this tendency, and no doubt that is true. Nevertheless the tendency is there. This business of borrowing money is like taking the

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell first drink, although I know the minister has not done that yet. You never know quite where you will stop.
We are at the end of what might be called fifteen years of boom times during which the government came along year after year and told us about the buoyant economy. How pleased they were to tell us of that. How good it has been for all of us that it was buoyant. Of course it was inevitable that they should take the credit for it. They were carried along on the crest of the wave and perhaps they hardly realized what was happening. But they took the credit and now it may be that they are going to have to have a reckoning. It may be that they are going to have to give a real accounting. Certainly it is relevant to ask how it is that after fifteen years of the kind of times we all remember, after the scores of billions of dollars that the government has taken from us, why after all this is it that with the economy quickened the picture is given to us by the minister of hundreds of millions which we will now have to pay by way of deficit. That is a question which I hope will be answered. I do not think the minister has answered it yet.
Reference has been made to the gross national product. The government has pretty nearly reached the stage when it almost holds itself able to control the gross national product, and I shall say a word about that later. If the gross national product does not behave as it is supposed to, then it is unfortunate, as the deficit could easily grow quite a lot.
I wonder what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the former Minister of Finance would say if they were here. They had some strong things to say a couple of years ago about deficits when our party was proposing to reduce taxes, not through deficits, although we were accused of that by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said that we had deficits in mind and it was natural for him to say that because after all there was nothing in his experience which would suggest that you should reduce taxes by making economies. In his experience you only reduce taxes when you are on a rising economy, when prices are high, when you have hundreds of millions of dollars more than you expected by reason of these high prices, and you are able to make certain tax reductions. As my colleague says, they were made on the eve of an election.
It is natural for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to feel that anyone who was going to reduce taxes was not going to do it by saving, but would do it by some other method. So the minister who did not think much of deficits accused us, quite unfairly, of having it 

in mind. As reported in the Globe and Mail of June 25, 1953, the minister said:
Deficit financing was just as dangerous for countries as it was for families who spent more than they earned.
Our good friend the former minister of finance also said in a broadcast, referring to borrowing money and running up the national debt-it was natural perhaps that he should say this because he had the delightful experience of being in office during a rising price economy and was able to show surpluses-and I think this is quite interesting:
This is in a very real sense buying your votes with your children's earnings for quite obviously your children will be paying that extra debt.
What a pity that those two ministers did not tell the present minister that his tax reductions should come from economies. It is too bad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not here today so that we might know just what he thinks about it. Perhaps we might get a judgment from the supreme court bench on it.
Is the government so bankrupt that in the face of difficulties that we all know we are facing now its only expedient is the old-fashioned one of debasing the currency? Borrowing is so seductive, and is a practice which should be closely watched, particularly, as I say, by the fixed income group and by farmers.
I think it is important to look behind the minister's words for a moment. He has not really taken us into his confidence. I am afraid that from the way he speaks we have had a sort of brushoff. Let us look for a moment at the gross national product figures on which he bases his calculations. Incidentally we should remind ourselves that the gross national product is a funny figure; it does not mean business done, it merely means goods produced. Conceivably you might have a terrific gross national product and still be very badly off if you could not sell it and deal with it. Of course it is a rough and ready guide because we do sell most of what we produce. But do not let us forget that the gross national product figure may contain, as it does now, millions of dollars of goods which remain unsold.
In 1953 the gross national product was $24-4 billion; in 1954 it had come down to $24 billion; and in 1955 we find the minister basing his budget on $25-25 billion, and he hopes it will reach a rate of $26 billion by the end of the year. That hope of course will be based on a bit of pump priming, if I may use that phrase in the minister's hearing.
We have a brand new way of setting taxes and making our estimates. We are doing it

I will leave that as a special perquisite of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). It becomes somewhat personal and I do not think it is suitable for this house.
I want to repeat again that the minister went out of his way to underline the fact that his budget was not intended to stimulate the economy. Oh, no; no nonsense of that kind; it did not need stimulating. Therefore that is equivalent to saying that the minister was not taking steps for the unemployed. I believe that he was not taking us into his confidence, that they were somewhere in his mind but that he did not feel quite free to talk about it. When I say this I have in mind these figures, and particularly the last figures which are worse than ever and which seem to me to be just a disgrace to us all, particularly the fact that we should have seven times as much unemployment as there is in England.
The unemployed are not forgotten citizens, but I am sure they must sometimes almost feel themselves to be rejected citizens, casualties of the industrial army, frightened men and women with cold bodies and hungry stomachs, as my colleague from Hamilton West said, who are afraid of what is going to happen to them.
Let us look back to what this government has done and has not done. We all remember the brave words of 1945 and the spring of 1946. They were words of hope; they were words not merely of economic significance but words of hope, sympathy and understanding. But apparently today the expression of real concern is left to us in the opposition. The government apparently is concerned with one thing, namely to try to slide from under. That is the only way 1 have been able to explain to myself what is happening. It is true that last September the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) used words which were the absolute antithesis of that. Indeed, they went so far that I cannot help wondering whether perhaps, being in his own
[Mr Macdonnell.]
bailiwick at that time, he may have had a little bit of, shall I say, adventitious enthusiasm which prompted him to go a little bit farther than he would have gone in more serious moments. The Prime Minister said this:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody, we are incompetent.
Those are extremely strong words. Since then I think it is true to say that there has been nothing but ignominious retreat. The attitude of the government since then, as compared with that statement, is as far removed from it as the east is from the west. It is hard now to remember the clarion call of last September or even to think that it was made. Since then we have had nothing except a feeble little toot.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have had increasing
incompetence.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have had an attitude of detachment. The unemployed are our fellow citizens. While we here in this house cannot deal with things in a sentimental way, regardless of business and regardless of financial considerations, nevertheless there is such a thing as an attitude of mind which I am sure will have its effect on our unfortunate fellow citizens. It has this effect, I know, on those who work most closely with them, namely, the social service workers. While they are often regarded as too sentimental, in my own family and elsewhere I happen to have close contact with them and I would say they are a very intelligent, wise group of men and women who do not deal only in sentimentality. When I read their memorandum on unemployment in greater Toronto I read something which it seems to me must be gall and wormwood to the unemployed. This is a memorandum which I received from Toronto and it has to do with the attitude of governments. I cannot help feeling sure one of the things that affect the unemployed most is that they are the unwanted people. They are tossed from one area of government to another. The memorandum reads:
The federal government maintains that it has met the main need through unemployment insurance; that constitutionally the responsibility for any residual program rests with the provinces and there is no evidence that the problem is beyond the capacities of the provinces.
The provincial government tells us that assistance to the employable unemployed is a federal responsibility. They refer to the proposals made by the federal government in 1945.
I shall also have occasion to refer to them.
They also contend that they lack the financial capacity to meet the problem. The government of

Ontario stresses the value of centralizing in one administration responsibility for both employment and unemployment.
The municipalities take the view that municipal revenues from property are unsuitable for meeting this need. They feel that it is unfair to the property owner to carry a responsibility which should be shared by all citizens. However, the city of Toronto has recently stated its willingness to share the cost of relief assistance and the services necessary in connection therewith with the federal and provincial governments on a 40-40-20 basis. There are twelve other municipalities in the greater Toronto area, some of which may not find it financially possible to enter into such an agreement.
As I said, and I do not wish to say this in any personal way, the question of real concern for the unemployed seems to have been left to us. When we talk with the government we seem to get into a world of statistics. Human beings seem to be remote shadows. How different it would be if the government were able to make real savings and to assist the provinces and the municipalities. After all, unemployment insurance is only a very partial solution. As we watched the government earlier in the session, as we noted the blank face they turn to all requests regarding unemployment, as we noted the ever more and more rapid retreat of the Prime Minister, as we listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), we all thought that action was being saved for the budget. We felt that the government would not dare to leave things as they were, that the budget would grapple with the situation. Well, we were wrong.
Here we have the budget and there is no report or explanation on this aspect of our affairs at all. As I said a moment ago, we have roughly seven times the proportion of unemployment in Britain. Why have we this plague, this disease? Is it want of flexibility? In the pioneer days people were free to go and expected to go across the country, if necessary, looking after themselves. But we have made it difficult, if not impossible, by our complicated machinery to move from one place to another. If a man goes to another municipality he may deprive himself of his rights to assistance.
Are we going to have to wait for the report of the new commission to be set up? Is that to be the intellectual answer to this intellectual bankruptcy that faces us so far? I am not going to sneer at the commission. I think there is a good deal to be said for having an outside view come and explore situations which are being handled by civil servants, however good they may be. I think there is an argument for that. On the other hand, I remember that a most high sounding
19, 1955
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell committee was set up at the beginning of the war which was never allowed to do much. I think its days were numbered from the first day it was appointed because I doubt very much if the civil servants ever intended that the committee should be effective.
What about the younger people? As I said a moment ago, it is much more difficult for them to move about the country as they could in simpler and more pioneer days. We have the bitter complaint, which I myself believe, that there is injurious overlapping between the citizenship and immigration and labour departments in respect of placements. I believe this is true, and I put it up to the ministers concerned to tell us the whole story frankly.
I can find no sense in the government's attitude of wait and see. Have they dug down into the basic causes? Have they probed maladjustment city by city, industry by industry? I know of no evidence. We have not had it in the house.
In the house we have really had irrelevant generalities. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that business is good. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) hopes for the best. The Prime Minister, at the national Liberal federation meeting, spoke of "woes" that were "temporary". That will not comfort the unemployed. They may very well say that life is temporary too. No reasoned hope has been held out. Various questions enter the mind. Do we need higher skills? I talked last night to a manufacturer who pointed out to me the extraordinary need of increasing the number of people with higher skills if we are to meet competition. The suggestion has even been made that, as a temporary measure no doubt, we should keep children in school longer in order to give them higher skills. There would be difficulties of accommodation there and maybe it is not practical.
I am just throwing out these suggestions because when we have such a situation confronting us it seems to me that everything should be tried. If everything is being tried, all I can say is that the House of Commons has not been advised. I might refer to the debate on unemployment long enough to say that I was amazed by the negation on the government side. Even the little things have not been done. Why could the minister not have remitted the sales tax on municipal corporations? It is not a new point to raise but I wonder whether it has been fully explored whether we cannot do more processing of raw materials at home. I know that is as old as the hills, but has it been fully explored? Of course we have got to

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell export a lot of iron ore and other things, but is it not possible for us to make the best of both worlds to some extent and manufacture more of our raw materials here?
Just the other day I heard of a case where a hardboard factory was set up and at the time it was established the United States tariff was 6| per cent. The factory was doing very well and making a very superior product when suddenly the tariff was raised to 16J per cent. That seems to me an unfriendly way for neighbours to carry on. That seems to me a case where there ought to be some possibility of compromise and accommodation. As we all know, in the province of Ontario real progress was made in respect of the export of raw wood. If these things have been done, if the situation has been fully explored, the house should know. I certainly am not informed as I should like to be. There is one special thing that I mention as I come to the end of this part of my speech. We seem to have made a sad mess in respect of one possible source of substantial employment. I refer of course to the pipe line. It seems that there we have just messed the thing up completely and lost for this year what might have been a very substantial source of employment.
A dominion-provincial conference is at last being grudgingly called. It is only an agenda conference, I understand. It is to get ready for the conference. It almost makes one despair when one wonders whether this is again a case of this year, next year, some time, never. I was present in the Senate chamber when the dominion-provincial conference was adjourned sine die around the 1st of May, 1946. At that time it was interesting, almost pathetic, to observe the desire of some of the provincial representatives, notably our friend Angus Macdonald who is no longer with us, to have the conference adjourned to a specific date. But no, it would not be conceded.
Now, it is hard to find any sign of enthusiasm on the part of this government in the preparations for the forthcoming conference. It seems to me their attitude has been one of twisting and squirming and trying by every means to avoid responsibility. Where are the brave days of 1945? The vision apparently has passed away. I know what has been said. It will be said that since then we have had to step up our defence expenditures. I know that very well, and a lot of other things have happened. The government is taking a couple of billion dollars more out of the taxpayers than they were at that time.
We go back to 1945. As I say, the vision has passed away like the snow in spring.

Let us remind ourselves of what was talked about seriously back in 1945. There were to be efforts directed to a high degree of employment; efforts directed to (1) export trade, (2) to private investment, (3) consumption, (4) expenditures and public investment. Governments then thought they could regulate the economy. I imagine now they would like to forget some of the brave words. I know that a gentleman not renowned for his opposition to the Liberal party, Bruce Hutchison, says that the minister is now on white fly paper, by which I understand he means that the minister is more or less stuck with some of the promises that were made in the past.
Now, let us consider for a moment what has happened since 1946. In his budget speech of 1946 Mr. Ilsley said that owing to the failure of the conference, which I described a moment ago, several of the major objectives must be held in abeyance for the time being. Then he added that "they remain, nevertheless, an essential part of the program of this government". On July 15,
1946,	that was just after Mr. Ilsley's speech, Prime Minister King wired to the premier of Saskatchewan that the federal government was "ready to explore mutually satisfactory arrangements in regard to the whole or any part of our earlier public investment and social security proposals." In 1947 Premier Hart said that Mr. King had assured him- I think this was when the British Columbia agreement was signed-that as soon as a sufficient number of provinces had signed agreements he would call another dominion-provincial conference to discuss various matters, including unemployment.
In his budget speech of 1947 Mr. Abbott said that "the government of Canada looks forward to the day when the agreement of all or substantially all the provinces will make possible the achievement of the great national purposes which impelled the dominion to make its comprehensive proposals of August 1945." He said that this included "the development of an efficient and flexible tax system designed to permit the expansion of employment and income." That was in
1947,	and those were brave words; but what about actions? Well, as I said a few minutes ago, the government seems to me to have been squirming and wriggling ever since to evade responsibility.
Perhaps there is one thing I should mention. I discovered to my surprise, and to the surprise of a lot of other people, a clause which is in the dominion-provincial tax agreements and which looks to me like a bit of slick legalism. I shall read it:
Nothing contained in this agreement shall be construed as an admission by either party to this

agreement that the said party is responsible ior the whole or any part of the cost of the relief of unemployment, either during the operation of this agreement or at any other time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether it is fair to call that a joker. I have met some people during the recess who certainly thought it was a joker. They had not known about it. They thought it was a curious place to have this matter of social policy introduced. Of course, it should be apparent to everybody that the effect of that was purely to benefit and protect the dominion. So far as the provinces are concerned, their responsibility comes under the British North America Act. They could not be relieved by this clause, so that we can take it this was what I call a slick legal device to protect the dominion. I do not think very highly of it because it would seem to me extremely likely that it was obtained under what might be called a mild amount of duress. The provinces were getting money at the moment and unemployment at that time was not a very serious matter. A bird in the hand was worth a good deal. However that may be, they signed that agreement.
Now, what do we find? I have read the memorandum from the social workers in Toronto pointing out that all governments were claiming they were not responsible. It is a sorry record. We had the visit of the Toronto board of control here, and they were told to go back and talk to the province. We had the request from British Columbia, and they were told that they had not established the fact they were unable to take care of the situation. It is a sorry record and the federal government cannot camouflage its half-hearted contribution.
Of course, as I said some time ago, these things come back, and usually to the purse. If the government had made savings, if they were able to do more, then the situation might be different. This brings me to the question of expenditures, savings and extravagance, on which I shall say a very few words. It is an old story and a sad story. We have had the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) compared to Hercules, but the reductions which have been made, on balance, are trivial, except in defence and finance. The finance reduction I understand is more or less temporary and accidental. The old sink holes are still infinitely capacious: professional and special services, telephones and telegrams and all the other things with which we are so familiar.
There is just one thing I am going to mention. It has already been mentioned in this
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell house but seems to me to be so fantastic I am going to mention it again. It is the case of the C.B.C. The C.B.C. has been made a little empire. It has taxes of its own. This takes us back past the days of the consolidated revenue fund when all taxes were earmarked for special purposes and when infinite inconvenience was caused thereby. As I say, the C.B.C. has an empire of its own and taxes of its own. In their last report we have the astounding situation that they had a surplus of $6'5 million. Of course, it was not a surplus at all but a combination of circumstances that had prevented them from making some capital expenditures which they had intended to make.
The best comment I can make on their situation and the way they carry on business is to read what the Auditor General had to say in his report. He had made suggestions to the C.B.C. as to their method of doing business. When you have an empire of your own, and taxes of your own, and when you do not have to come each year to have your estimates approved in this house, I suppose you do become pretty uppish. And evidently the C.B.C. at any rate took precious little stock of what the Auditor General had said, and caused him to make this comment:
Subsequent action by the corporation-
This is subsequent to his suggestion of change, which was ignored.
Subsequent action by the corporation not having been of a nature to remedy the situation, the manner in which the accounts were kept during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1954, was not found to be conducive to satisfactory auditing.
Mr. Speaker, I ask you and I ask myself if anything more conducive to abuse and more contrary to common sense in dealing with large sums of money could be imagined. I suppose someone had the bright idea that there would be a certain narrow logic in letting the users of radio and television carry the burden of the C.B.C., as we were doing away with licence fees. This was a bright idea. I suppose it was thought that it would be painless. Of course anyone who looked at the realities would see there was no reason whatsoever, no reason in the world, to expect that the tax would be the right amount: and there was even less reason to expect that if it was too large there would be any complaint from the C.B.C.
But even now when the foolishness looks so self-evident, and when as I say they have a phony surplus of $6,500,000-even now, apparently there is no disposition to change. Indeed, the answer that is given to us is that this year the C.B.C. will be able to spend the full amount. I do not know how they figure what it will be, because that would

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell depend upon the amount of sales. But whatever it is, they will do their best-and I think probably we can rely upon them for that.
I can only repeat that when the government deals with money in this way, to use the Prime Minister's expression, it is not smart enough. And this is what caused some newspapers, I think, to call this an irresponsible budget. It is neither one thing nor another. It does little enough for its beneficiaries, and nothing to ease the burden of the lowest income groups in the community, who get no reduction of any kind, and who will have to help pay the taxes to repay the borrowed money.
Notwithstanding the optimistic predictions, we have deficit financing. I have read to the house the criticisms by other ministers with regard to deficit financing. We have tax reductions which are to come from borrowing. It is so much easier to borrow, and so we have set out on the slippery path of inflation, notwithstanding the fact that the minister tells us that times are good-and it is likely he would add that they are to be almost unimaginably better.
As for the real problem, that of unemployment-well, the budget virtually ignores it. They are looking to a dominion-provincial conference, as, if and when it takes place. We can only hope that the lukewarm and indifferent attitude of the government will be changed. That can come about only through the efforts of this house, supported by public opinion.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in its budget proposals the government has failed:
(a)	to give effective stimulus to Canadian enterprise to create employment and opportunity;
(b)	to reduce taxation affecting those on low incomes and allowances;
(c)	to curb its own extravagance and inefficiency ;
(d)	to recognize the serious position in which the Canadian farmer and other producers now find themselves."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to discuss the minister's budget I would say at first that, despite the able manner in which he delivered it, it was a most deceptive document, for it failed utterly to suggest any remedies for the situation that has arisen as a result of the drop in farm income and the serious level of unemployment-which are the real factors behind the latest recession in the Canadian economy.
One excuse, that the 1954 drop in the gross national production and of farm income is

due to a poor western crop last year, is both misleading and fallacious. The poor crop has had relatively little influence yet, because of the small quotas of deliveries that have been permitted from it. There is-and I do not think this fact is generally recognized-a very substantial amount of good wheat lying on the farms of western Canada.
I have a letter which illustrates that point. It comes from the co-operative farm in my constituency on the Matador ranch, which is operated by some 17 veterans from the last war, and their families, on a co-operative basis. After referring to the distribution of cars at local elevators and protesting against being compelled to deliver grain at non-pool elevators-and may I say this is a very real grievance among our farmers in western Canada who wish to deliver their grain to the pool elevators system, their own organization-the writer goes on to say this:
As far as our farm is concerned, we have about 14,000 bushels of 1952 wheat; 15,000 bushels of 1953 wheat and several thousands of bushels of 1954 wheat, so don't let the government in power get away with the idea that the poor 1954 wheat crop is the reason for the present farm plight. There is plenty of 1952 and 1953 wheat besides our poor grade 1954 wheat.
He then goes on to say this:
We had hail damage of 43 per cent in 1953 and also some damage in 1952. As I regretfully say- here we are more fortunate than several of our neighbouring farmers who were not hailed. We were able to get hail insurance on wheat we would never have been able to sell or build storage for. Some have welcomed the hail so as to collect hail insurance as they have no faith in the way the present government in power has lost markets.
To identify the letter may I say that it was written by Mr. E. P. Monson of the co-operative farm at Matador; and of course this letter is available to the house, if it wishes to have it.
Thus, the minister's excuse regarding one aspect of the fall in our economy is, as I have said, quite fallacious. Nor should we allow it to be said-and I wish to make this point clear-that the policies of the pool, of the wheat board and the farm organizations are responsible for the loss of our overseas markets.
At no time was Canadian wheat held off the market to claim higher prices from Great Britain or from other overseas customers under the international wheat agreement. Great Britain, for example, was free to buy wheat from Argentina, Turkey, the Danubian countries, or any non-member of the agreement. Nor can the surplus of Canadian wheat be caused by this agreement or the operations of the wheat board. Wheat acreage in Canada has declined over three million acres between 1949 and 1954. Importing countries increased their own production not because

of the international wheat agreement but because they wished to increase and subsidize their domestic production. Wheat in Britain, France and Italy has always been higher in price than under the international wheat agreement. When No. 2 northern wheat on the farm in my constituency in Saskatchewan was $1.60 a bushel, the British farm price rose from $1.99 to $2.28 a bushel. That happened between 1950 and 1953. I may say that these are the latest figures available to me. Prices in France rose from $2.01 to $2.83 a bushel in exactly the same period. Only the bringing into relationship of the sterling price with that of the dollar will bring about a change. This desirable convertibility, as it is called, will come only when North America imports more commodities from our potential customers and thus improves the trading relationship. Government policies to promote this alone can improve our wheat exports. May I say that I saw no such policies foreshadowed in the budget.
Those who would destroy commodity agreements in order to restore speculative marketing are offering no solution to the Canadian farm people or that of agricultural producers anywhere in the world. Therefore, the budget speech of the minister fails completely to recognize the real fall in the economy when it suggests that it is in large measure owing to the poor wheat crop of 1954. In my opinion, the budget fails to meet national needs in respect to two problems: the fall in farm income and the tremendous rise in unemployment, which I believe are not really two problems but are two sides of one problem. If we wish to be at all alarming, today's news of the latest dominion bureau of statistics unemployment figure of
633.000	people registered for work should alarm us. It is the highest figure for many, many years. I did not quite get the other figures of those actually out of work which were also broadcast, but they were well over
400.000	on March 19.
The minister's estimate of the gross national product seems to me altogether too optimistic. Even the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) does not do more than estimate the capital expenditure program which, while somewhat higher than in 1954, will still be lower than in 1953. The Minister of Finance believes that we shall not only recover our loss in production of last year but in this year we shall add to it and make what is in effect a very abnormal gain in the gross national product. Upon that assumption he bases his estimated deficit of $160 million at the end of the present financial year.
I want to say again that there was no reference in the budget to the 600,000 who
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell were unemployed at that time, 633,000 now. These are the unplaced applicants for work. The only reference is to be found in this one sentence of the budget speech. The minister said at page 2728 of Hansard:
In recent years we have become so accustomed to big improvements in production, that even a minor reversal of the trend is apt to cause more concern than the situation warrants.
Surely, 10 per cent or more of our entire labour force seeking work, or unemployed, should not be regarded as a minor reversal. Certainly, that is not the opinion of the workers, and above all it is not the opinion of an unemployed person.
The minister persuades himself that production levels for last year were next to the record. It is true that because of the growth in population and the monetary inflation during the post-war period, the absolute figure of gross national production has been increasingly satisfactory to the minister when presenting the budget. However, the present minister and the government should follow the example of the government's own bureau of statistics and express the gross national product in terms of constant dollars and then examine Canadian production today and compare it with the previous years to get the comparable per capita figure.
The gross national product per capita, in terms of constant dollars, that is the value of a dollar between 1935 and 1939, which is the base period that the dominion bureau of statistics takes, was in 1954, not just lower than in 1953, as appears to be the case when we consider only the absolute figures, but in constant dollars it was actually lower than 1953, 1952, and 1951, and it is indeed the lowest since 1950, when the Korean war broke out and we got a boost in production.

If we go back farther we find that the gross national product per capita, in constant dollars, was in fact higher in 1943, 1944 and 1945, than it was in 1954. I think that is right. Indeed, these figures underline the contention that I have made over and over again in this house that the Canadian production machine functions best during times of war or of post-war defence preparation. Of course, that is not the fault of the machine. Productively, our scientists, our engineers and
2956	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell our workers have increased their productivity year by year, but our economy has been unable to adjust itself to consuming all of which it is capable of producing except, as I have said, during heavy wartime or for defence preparedness. Therefore, there is really no overproduction. The unplanned economy fails to move the wealth of the nation to those who need it, and accordingly, there is waste and poverty in the midst of world-wide actual or potential plenty.
Now, this is where the budget has its part to play. There are two things which the budget could do, two related things which the minister failed to do. First, tax relief should be given in such a way as to most effectively stimulate consumption. Second, the budget should plan to enable the government to initiate large public investment programs to fill the gap when private investment fails.
Now, with regard to the stimulation of consumption, the budget does very little in this respect. We welcome even the parsimonious tax reductions that are to benefit the lower income groups. We welcome the reduction in the excise tax on automobiles and the abolition of the tax on tires and tubes. With the rapid growth in suburban living and the distances between our farms and their sources of supply, the automobile has become an absolute necessity rather than a luxury for large sections of the population.
I am disappointed that the minister did not reduce the rate of sales tax or even make wide exemptions from the tax of commodities like clothing and household effects. The sales tax, including the social security tax of 2 per cent, is 10 per cent at the federal level, but because it is pyramided as it passes from the manufacturer to the consumer, the increase in cost to the consumer is considerably more than 10 per cent. Indeed, in some circumstances it may even be 20 per cent or more than 20 per cent, though of course it is not always that amount.
One of the ways of increasing the purchase of consumption goods would have been to reduce the sales tax. The minister made some reductions in income tax which are expected to reduce the federal revenues by some $85 million in the current fiscal year. These reductions will, of course, not assist those who are unemployed nor those who do not pay income tax.
May I say to the minister that this was done in a most misleading manner. When we heard the minister we jumped to the conclusion that the reduction in the tax was more substantial in the lower brackets than in the higher income brackets. What the minister actually did, in spite of any impression to the contrary which was contained in the table which I looked at the night the 

budget was placed before us, was to reduce the tax rate by two percentage points in all personal income brackets. This means that the married taxpayer with two children receiving family allowance and earning $3,000 a year gets a tax reduction of $7 for the whole of 1955, or an average of 58 cents a month. In other words, slightly less than two cents a day. I do not think that anyone will argue that that will stimulate consumption substantially.
The married man with two children receiving family allowance with an income of $100,000 a year will receive a tax reduction of nearly $1,000, or to be precise, $977. The higher the income the more rebate that is received. This is a reversal of what the table included in the budget seemed to indicate when I looked at it the night the budget was placed before us.
Now to achieve the maximum of benefit to the economy, benefits should have been higher in the lower income group than in the higher. The best way to have done this would have been to have increased the basic exemptions to say $1,500 for single persons and $3,000 for married persons, with of course corresponding exemptions in relation to dependents. Had this been done the married taxpayer with two children earning $3,000 a year would have received a reduction of $105 instead of the $7 he will receive this year.

I shall come to that in a
moment. In all the higher brackets increases should have been made to compensate to some extent for the loss of revenue due to the higher exemptions. While I cannot go into it as I would like to if time permitted, this could have been accomplished by the imposition of a capital gains tax. People in this country who have been dealing in stocks over the past several years have made huge incomes and those incomes have not been taxable.
The minister could have helped the small man too by the removal of the 3 per cent floor on medical expenses. The House of Commons expressed itself in favour of its removal some years ago and the government I think should be censured for having failed to carry out the recommendations of the representatives of the people of Canada so clearly expressed in this parliament at the time. If the minister is able to reduce the income tax on the higher income groups and on large corporations then he certainly could afford to adopt this proposal which would benefit primarily the low and middle income groups.

The government is by slow degrees introducing what is in effect a more regressive personal income tax structure, ignoring more and more the basis of ability to pay. Recent budgets have whittled steadily away at this principle. Let me make my point clear by comparing the tax rate for 1956 with that in effect in 1949 when the present scale of exemptions was established.
In 1949 a married man with no children earning $3,000 a year paid a tax of approximately $150; in 1956 a married taxpayer earning the same amount will also pay approximately $150. In 1949 a married taxpayer with no children and earning $5,000 paid a tax of approximately $510; in 1956 he will pay $510. In 1949 a childless married taxpayer earning $10,000 paid an income tax of approximately $1,660; in 1956 the same taxpayer will pay a tax of about $1,560, a reduction of $100. A person earning $100,000 paid a tax in 1949 of $50,360, but in 1956 he will pay $48,460, a reduction of $1,900.
The minister may say that this is due to the operation of the old age security tax. That is true very largely and that is my point. This situation arises because of the $60 limit on the old age security tax. A person with a taxable income of $3,000 will pay $60 just as the man with a taxable income of $10,000, $20,000 or $100,000 will pay the same $60. This means that at the lower income the old age security tax is 2 per cent, but in the $10,000 bracket it is six-tenths of 1 per cent and in the $20,000 bracket it is three-tenths of 1 per cent. This illustrates what I mean when I say that our income tax structure has become more and more regressive. If we must have a special old age security tax of this type, then remove the ceiling. Make it 2 per cent all the way through, which would help to get the fund out of the red.
I should say immediately that I am glad that the government has abandoned the fiction that old age security will be paid for by this tax. We never supported the proposal to set up what is in effect a separate fund to meet this special need. There was no more logic in that than there would have been in setting up separate funds to meet

I made a comparison between the personal income tax in effect in 1949 and that which will be in effect in 1956. In 1949 the tax credit allowed receivers of dividends from Canadian corporations was first introduced. At first 10 per cent of what was received in dividends on shares was deductible from the income tax otherwise payable by a taxpayer. In 1953 this tax credit was increased to 20 per cent producing, as I pointed out at the time, the fantastic result that a married man with no children who received all his income from clipping coupons could receive up to $9,760 free of personal income tax. That was the position in the 1954 taxation year.
As a result of the taxation changes proposed by the minister this year the results are even more fantastic. The government has been most lavish in benefiting this group of coupon clippers. As a result of the tax concession for 1956 when the tax changes will have their full effect the minister will have increased the $9,760 free of income tax to $11,133.33 which the coupon clipper may receive in dividends before paying any personal income tax. To my mind this is personal income tax evasion, quite legitimate but on a mammoth scale, marking an addition of almost $1,400 to the income which this group may receive tax exempt.

This seems to me entirely inequitable when we consider that an earned income of $3,000 will pay $150 in income tax, while someone who receives his income from Canadian securities may receive $11,133 and pay no personal income tax at all. To argue, as the minister may, that corporations are taxed is entirely beside the point. I might just as well argue that because the Canadian Pacific Railway pays corporation taxes, then its wage earners should pay no income tax. I could just as well argue that proposition. Surely when we consider that corporation taxes are being reduced and that the income earner is of more use to society than is the coupon clipper, this iniquitous differential should be wiped out.
My second criticism was that the budget has failed to perform a second important function, namely preparation for a vast program of public investment. The minister was much concerned about the impact of corporation income tax. That he feels more concerned in that regard than in regard to individuals is evidenced by his decision to make the corporation income tax reduction retroactive to January 1 while the personal income tax changes will not become effective until July 1.
Concern for corporations no doubt is, in the minister's opinion, designed to stimulate investment. The first thing that must be pointed out is that the nature of corporation investment is changing. For instance, the 1954 preliminary figures indicate that gross business savings, presumably available for investment, and depreciation allowances were almost four times as large as were what might be called undistributed corporation profits. Accordingly the importance of the size of corporation profits is not as significant as it once may have been. Business has often refused to invest regardless of what its total profits may be. Consequently, reductions in corporation tax at this time, instead of going into new investments, may be paid in large part in the form of dividends, swelling the tax exempt status of certain people and providing them with what may be regarded as the guaranteed annual wage for coupon clippers. May I add that these same coupon clippers are often those who oppose most strenuously the idea of a guaranteed annual wage for the workers in industry.
It seems to me that the minister should have left the corporation taxes as they were, and should have diverted the revenues and capital gains into social investments of many types. That course indeed would have stimulated the economy. It would have demonstrated that the government was more


concerned with social investment than with the financial interests. This revenue, as I suggested, plus an unearned capital gains tax, could have been used to assist the provinces to build hospitals and schools, to provide local amenities, to establish a vigorous national housing plan and, indeed, perhaps even a national health plan and so on. It might have helped in a national highway aid program, although this is considerably less potent in the economy in terms of employment than is the construction of houses and institutions such as those I have mentioned.
In order to emphasize the point I am going to move the following subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
"(e) to provide assistance to the provincial governments in order to enable them to plan their financing in such a manner as to relieve the people of this country from the crushing load of heavy municipal taxation."
I think that subamendment points up exactly what I have been saying. Some of our banks, it will be observed, notably in a recent monthly review of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, recognize the need for social investment of this kind to meet the needs of our people and to build a more prosperous Canada. The need for a public investment program has been underlined, of course, because of unemployment in recent months.
Municipalities have been forced, by the failure of the federal government to act, to adopt makeshifts. A short time ago the Toronto city council announced a work program which would enable unemployed men to earn $20 a week. This program reminded me of similar relief programs during the early days of the depression, which programs members of the Liberal party in common with some of the rest of us denounced from one end of this country to the other.
Of course this program will be of some help to those who are unable to find work, for it will assist them in obtaining food and a minimum of lodging, but can this be regarded from any angle as satisfactory? Is this a stimulus to purchasing power and our national economy? Is this indeed to any degree the honouring of promises that were made during the war by the federal government-particularly following the Rowell-Sirois commission-to assume responsibility for the unemployed employables? How can it be regarded as just and right that failure to plan our economic system should first deny to the unemployed the right to perform useful work that they are capable and trained to

perform, and then force them to work at substandard wages-$20 a week-in order to exist?
Hence, rather than the reduction in corporation income taxes I should like to have seen at least a start on a vigorous public investment policy to provide opportunities for full employment. When private enterprise finds that it cannot profit by expanding its investment and production programs, the government is obliged to resort to promises and concessions.	This is like enticing a
donkey by holding a carrot before its nose. If private investors are unwilling to accept risks without government guarantees such as were demanded recently in the proposed building of a trans-Canada gas pipe line, a government investment board should fill the need. When large corporations fail to justify their oft-repeated faith in the future of Canada with deeds, then we should have a national investment board to meet the need for social investment.
That has been clearly demonstrated this winter. Instead of making concessions to corporations the federal government should be doing the job that corporations fail to do, and instead of guaranteeing them regarding future profits or the safety of their bonds, it should take whatever profits may accrue for the benefit of the Canadian people.
In connection with this pipe-line discussion, may I add once more-as I did when the matter came before the house some time ago-that it is intolerable that the head of a United States corporation, in this instance Gulf Oil Company, should refuse to have anything to do with a project in which the people of Canada might have some control, which the government demanded quite properly because of the financial risk the government of Canada was requested to take. I hope the government will remain firm in refusing to accept the dictatorship of any powerful corporation, whether it be Canadian, commonwealth or foreign. It is this parliament and this parliament alone which should make decisions affecting the welfare of Canada and its people, and not profit-seeking corporations, domestic or foreign.
We welcome the proposal to set up a royal commission to examine prospects for the future development of Canadian resources and the Canadian economy, but it can do little in the way of immediate help. What we need is immediate action and a continuous program of economic development conscientiously and intelligently planned in a democratic way by the people as a whole, to meet the needs of the people. That surely should be a function of this parliament.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
I cannot go into other matters of great interest to the Canadian people, inasmuch as my time is drawing to a close. An opportunity will probably present itself to discuss the unusual type of tax reduction which applies only to one province. Let me say at once that some people have said that in attacking this concession to the government of Quebec we are attacking either the province or the people of the province to which it happens at the moment to apply. That is not so. As a matter of fact I would be as much concerned about this type of tax concession if it applied to my home province of Saskatchewan. To my mind the new law which is to come into effect this year introduces into the Canadian tax structure the dangerous precedent that federal income tax may vary from province to province.
I do not think that can be denied. No matter what the government may say, that is the effect of the proposal. The minister may say there is a provincial income tax in the province affected. Certainly there is. But the provincial income tax is levied on a different base, with higher exemptions than the federal tax, and there need be no necessary relationship between the two. The fact is that there is a unilateral reduction in the federal income tax that applies to one province which is, I may say, of special advantage to the high income groups in that province. That the reduction for Quebec was coupled with an invitation to any other province to break the tax rental agreements and enter into a similar arrangement is an invitation to undermine the whole basis of the tax rental agreements. These agreements are needed, and I believe everybody in the house thinks they are needed, particularly when broad fiscal powers of the national government are urgently needed to be exercised.
When the economy is threatened with recession, as indicated by falling farm prices and unemployment, that is the time when broad federal fiscal powers are most necessary; yet it is at this very time that the federal government itself has, in my opinion, weakened the national power to deal effectively with the national economic situation. However, I must leave this problem to some future debate.
A federal-provincial conference is pending. I hope this matter will be placed high on the agenda, and that ways and means will be found to strengthen rather than weaken the tax rental agreements because in many of our provinces, particularly those that are underprivileged through lack of natural resources, these tax rental agreements are of vital importance. If we are to have an even
2960	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Low
basis of opportunity for Canadians who live in various parts of Canada to enjoy the social services and other amenities of life which are their due, then we must have some method of spreading over the whole country the result of the productive enterprise of the country. The tax rental agreements were an attempt to do that, and I think they were successful to a remarkable degree. I am very disturbed to see what I consider to be a retreat from those agreements, indeed an undermining of them.
Of course I understand that when the conference meets, settles the agenda and meets again, tax rental agreements or some agreements must be negotiated or re-negotiated, let me add, with due regard of course to the rights and responsibilities of the provinces. But the provinces must also recognize that the welfare of all Canada is dependent upon the ability of this parliament and the government to meet successfully economic and social problems that are national in scope and importance. When confederation was established in 1867 the economic problems of the country were very different from what they are today. Yet the fathers of confederation in their wisdom saw to it that while the provinces were given the right to levy direct taxation all forms of taxation, including direct taxation, were to remain within the scope of the federal parliament.
In other words the fathers of confederation recognized, even in those days when the problems were few and simple, that this parliament must have the right to raise revenues in any way it saw fit to meet national needs. The tax rental agreements were a recognition that, while we had that right, nonetheless we were prepared to negotiate with the provinces with regard to a form of tax-income tax-which some of them had used, some only very recently, including the province of Quebec. Because of that it seems to me at this time, with the economy in its present condition and having in mind what may face us in the near future, that it is essential that we shall have tax agreements that will guarantee to all Canadians equality of opportunity from one end of the country to the other. Anything which tended to undermine that or to prevent this parliament handling national economic problems would, in my opinion, be fatal to the welfare of Canada and would bring about national disunity to a greater extent than we have known in the past.
We hope most sincerely that the federal government will not retreat from the right to organize the economy to meet the needs of the people of the country in whatever province they may live. Therefore we must have the necessary power, the necessary funds, to meet 

successfully economic and social problems that are national in scope and importance.
I see that my time has expired, but before I sit down let me say once again that in our opinion the budget and the proposals contained therein are unsatisfactory and fail completely to meet the conditions of falling farm prices, falling farm income, unemployment and other pressing needs of the country at the present time.
