speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rules of the house do not permit this group to move a subamendment; consequently there will be only the two already moved, one by the Progressive Conservatives and the other by the C.C.F. I looked over these amendments when they were handed to me on being moved by the hon. gentlemen, and because of the fact that each draws attention to the need for censuring the government on the various points mentioned we feel we must give our support to both.
I should like to say at this point that, in addition to censuring the government for its failure to meet the needs of the present situation, as was mentioned by the last speaker, the federal government should now be giving very careful attention to its plans for the dominion-provincial conference which is to convene shortly. Certainly if the provinces of this country are to discharge fully the responsibilities placed upon them by confederation, they must have the wherewithal with which to do so, and every effort will have to be made to see that they do have the finances. Otherwise I see no way in which the municipalities of the country, which have been carrying an undue burden of taxation during the past several years, can possibly be relieved.
I certainly join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in his appeal to the government to make certain that sufficient finances are made available to the provinces through some equitable means, tax agreements if you like, such as may be devised at the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference. It is because these things have not been provided for in the past that I feel I must support the subamendment and the amendment criticizing the government's lack of action.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the central message of my hon. friend's first budget is a half-hearted apology to the Canadian people, as if this budget were saying to them: the opposition in parliament have done so much talking about a business decline and serious unemployment during the past several months that we have come to half believe it ourselves. Consequently we are making some

changes in our financial policy for the coming year to help meet whatever these foolish people on the other side seem to think is wrong. There is no evidence, however, in the minister's budget to indicate that the government has come to fully realize just exactly what the situation is, and how serious it is.
The provisions of the budget do represent some change from the government's position of a year ago or even six months ago, but it is not enough to be able yet to call it repentance. Repentance, in my judgment, involves restitution. I have searched carefully through my hon. friend's budget and I can find only an indication here and there of half-hearted restitution to those who have been caused serious loss and worry, perhaps even extended suffering, as a consequence of government policies that have been allowed to carry on much longer than they should have been. I do think that budgeting for a deficit is exactly what the economy needs at the present time to help it pull out of the slump, and perhaps help to stimulate a higher economic activity so that unemployment can be abolished. I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) on that point.
I must give the Minister of Finance credit for having recognized that necessity at least. I might say right here that when the minister recognizes the necessity of budgeting for a deficit now, he recognized the necessity of seeing to it that more purchasing power was left in the hands of the people so they could buy some of the goods that are available. It is not with his proposal to budget for a deficit that we quarrel. Our criticism is that the tax cuts he made were not well distributed, and they were not designed to give relief to all the people who deserve to have relief at this time. It is clear that the Minister of Finance knew, perhaps as a consequence of the talk of unemployment and business decline from this side of the house, that the economy did need some sort of a shot in the arm.
I have noticed that quite a number of newspapers in the country since April 5 have called the minister's budget a shot in the arm. Well, I dispute that very strongly. About the best anyone could possibly say in that regard is that the budget does provide a very mild hypodermic, but I am afraid it has nothing more than milk in it. I would say the minister realized he had to provide the economy with a balance wheel, but our criticism is that he failed to equip the balance wheel with the proper loads. The minister must realize, I think, that unless you keep a balance wheel well loaded with those very interesting little well placed weights on the rim it
Private Bills
does not work smoothly, and it does not do the job it was designed to do. So it is with our economy. If you are going to provide it with a balance wheel you have to keep your balance wheel loaded. I shall talk about the the loads I have in mind just a little later.
Inasmuch as today is private members' day, Mr. Speaker, from five o'clock until six, may I ask you at this stage to call it five o'clock and I shall resume after the dinner hour.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has been suggested that hon. members went through the business for private members' hour quickly in order to have the privilege of hearing my speech. I hardly believe that is true. However, we are very grateful that we can carry on without too much of a break.
I have mentioned already that we think the Minister of Finance did the right thing when he budgeted for a deficit this year. But the important thing for hon. members to keep in mind is the manner in which he intends to finance that deficit. If he is going to run the country into debt by the issuance of bonds, either to the general public or through the chartered banks of the country, then we feel that is wrong. We contend that in any action the circumstances call for this year, if the minister is going to budget for a deficit then he must be prepared to finance that deficit without running the country into a further burden.
He can do that, as we have pointed out time after time. But we say he has used the proper method in attempting to meet the situation, at least partially, this year. We do think if he had really intended to give the economy the shot in the arm, the effective one that the newspapers have talked about, he should have gone further than he did. A deficit of $160 million in a $25 billion economy is a pretty weak hypodermic any way you want to look at it. We think the minister could very well have gone as far as $300 or $400 million of a deficit with perfect safety this year at least, until Canada returned to a high level of economic activity.
There are good reasons for taking that attitude. The government is depending almost entirely upon tax reductions to pull Canada out of the business slump and to cure the serious unemployment problem. At least that is the way it looks to us, unless they bring in some rather substantial supplementary estimates in June providing for much greater government investment than any of us have seen or suspected thus far. And so, as I say, tax cuts of only $148 million in a $25 billion economy, under such circumstances as we now face, when business has been somewhat depressed and unemployment in various sections of our country is very serious, are entirely inadequate to meet the needs. That is one of the reasons we propose voting for the amendment and the subamendment.
We do congratulate the minister upon the tax cuts he did make. We think it was wise to reduce income tax rates. But the minister

must realize that when he confines his reductions to the rate structure only he leaves out a great many people who deserve consideration, because there are many thousands of people in Canada whose incomes are below the income tax exemptions. What has the budget done for them? What has the budget done for old age pensioners, for those who are on superannuation, for the veterans on pensions and the like? Perhaps the minister felt that it was impossible to make any substantial change in exemptions under the Income Tax Act. I am inclined to believe that it was better not to try to do it this year. But we do think it would have been much more effective as a budget if, in addition to the income tax reductions the minister made, he had provided for some cuts in the sales tax. That would have made it possible for people in lower income groups to have at least some relief, and would have spread the favours at least more evenly. That is exactly where the purchasing power is most needed, among those people in the lower income groups.
I think perhaps the most serious criticism I can offer of the whole budget is that the minister failed to make any reduction in sales tax. I say this for a number of very important reasons. In the first place I think I have already mentioned that with the reduction in income tax rates he will not help the people who are not in income tax brackets- and in this I include old age pensioners, recipients of war veterans allowances and of veterans pensions, low wage earners-of whom there are many thousands. The reduction in the sales tax would have made it possible for them to retain a bit more of their already too meagre purchasing power, so they could do their share toward buying the surplus of goods that has accumulated throughout the country, and at the same time of course increase their own enjoyment of life to a certain extent. That would have been considerably more like real justice to all parts of the Canadian population than has been brought about by the minister in his budget.
There is another important reason, too, why I think the minister should have brought in some reduction in the sales tax at this time. We have developed a high price economy which is making it much more difficult than before for Canada to compete successfully in world trade. Anything, I contend, that will help to adjust consumer prices downward would stimulate trade and help to move more of our surplus goods to foreign markets. A reduction of the sales tax would be one means of helping to bring down some consumer prices to that end. We think the minister and the government lost a golden
The Budget-Mr. Low
opportunity right here and, as I say, in our judgment this is the most serious criticism we make of the financial proposals in the budget.
There were some slight excise tax cuts provided, but they were only slight, and they touched only a very restricted portion of the goods upon which the tax is imposed. We are glad to see the reductions, of course, the reduction from 15 per cent to 10 per cent in the excise tax on automobiles, and the abolition of the tax on truck and automobile tires no matter for what purpose they are used.
These are all to the good, and I am sure the Canadian people generally will welcome these tax reductions. But right here I do wish to voice serious criticism of the method the government has of handling some of these excise tax cuts. I think their method is quite unfair to retailers, such as automobile dealers. Taxes are payable at the factory, which means that when the automobile dealer takes cars from the factory into his storeroom or storage lot, he pays the tax before he can take them out. When the government announces in its budget, as it did on April 5, that there will be absolutely no refunds on taxes already paid at the factory on automobiles taken out by retailers, but remaining unsold, I say it is acting unfairly.
I remind the government that they have gotten into a very bad practice in the past number of years, namely the practice of making everybody but the government tax collectors for the government. Anyone might think the government would be rather grateful to have these people performing this gratuitous and difficult service. But how does the government show its gratitude? Well, in the case of automobile dealers, at least, they show it by dispensing a fairly substantial measure of unfairness and injustice, causing many of them serious loss.
I know of one dealer right in this city of Ottawa who had paid $8,000 in taxes at the factory in respect of cars he had already put into storage by budget day and that had remained unsold. But when the announcement of the tax cut was made he could expect no refund, and had to sell his cars in competition with other businesses in the city. Consequently he is suffering a considerable amount of injustice. I would think it would be possible for the government to find some means of preventing this kind of unfairness. I repeat that the method of handling the tax cut, particularly the cut in the excise tax, is very unfair to some of our retail dealers.
Since April 5, when the budget was brought down, there has been considerable discussion about whether Canada will be able to achieve

The Budget-Mr. Low
the $26 billion rate of gross national production this year. That was the aim set by the minister in his calculations. The official critic of the Progressive Conservative party has called the budget an excursion into unreality, I suppose because of the $26 billion figure as well as for some other reasons. Well, we should ask ourselves what chance the government has of achieving the $26 billion rate.
In the first place let me point out that we do have a great many unemployed in this country, and if the government will get busy and bring in policies designed to get them back to work they will contribute substantially toward the gross national production that we need to reach if we are to realize the plans in our present budget. Certainly by adopting policies which will put them back to work the government will have a better chance of realizing that $26 billion rate.
Another point to keep in mind is this. The minister has provided in the budget certain incentives to business to expand operations and to plow back into business more of the profits. Well, I agree with the need for providing those incentives. I think the minister was wise to make a reduction in the corporation income tax this year. Whether the 4 per cent reduction in corporation income tax will provide sufficient incentive to cause allout production, I would not be able to say. And when I use the figure "4 per cent" I mean that the amount of the reduction will be 4 per cent of the present rate. I understand the reduction is from 49 per cent to 47 per cent, which would be about 4 per cent over all.
I am rather inclined to believe that this will not be enough. It will be some stimulus, but I do not think it will be enough. We have kept business generally in this country on a very high rate of income tax for a long time. Whenever you impose a burden of tax that takes from the corporations every year about half of their profits you leave them very little with which to carry on the necessary expansion and new development to keep pace with a growing economy- perhaps I had better say to give impetus to the economy, to make it grow; for it is entirely through private and corporation investment that our economy is expected to grow and expand.
I am not going to argue at this point that the amount of corporation income tax reduction was too small. I am inclined to believe that it could have been a bit more without any serious dislocation in the government's plan, and certainly something more than the 4 per cent would have produced considerably

more incentive for expansion and development toward the $26 billion rate of gross national production which we hope to reach before the end of the year.
There is a third point to consider in this matter. If we get a good crop this year throughout the farming areas, and I sincerely hope we shall, then I believe we can reach the rate mentioned by the minister. But the greatest weakness of the budget, in my judgment, is its failure to provide adequate markets for our production. If we do reach the $26 billion rate of gross national production, what are we going to do with it? That is the big question. It seems to me that is the thing the government must face squarely sooner or later, and I suggest that now is the time to face it. What shall we do with all the production, if through incentive we spark an all-out effort and succeed in reaching the $26 billion rate of gross national production in 1955? I am not going to labour the point; I shall have something more to say about this matter of internal markets and balance wheels and loading the balance wheels just a little later on, but I do sincerely hope that we reach the objective that has been set by the minister.
The government has loaded its budget with a heavy burden of fixed charges which leaves it very little elasticity to meet the ups and downs of economic fluctuations. This fact increases the responsibility of the Minister of Finance and the government generally. It must eventually use more skill, managerial skill, than it ever used before in its history. It must become more conscious of the role which government must play in these times; otherwise, the fluctuations in the economy will become so violent as to make it impossible for the government to meet that burden of fixed charges without plunging the country into an impossible burden of public debt.
The minister said in his budget speech that two-thirds of all of the civil or nondefence expenditures provided in the budget were for public welfare, social security measures, for servicing the public debt and for paying provincial subsidies and tax rental payments. This does not leave very much elasticity, as I said, and it does impose the very heavy burden of fixed charges on everybody. With that in mind, it seems perfectly clear to me that the government in the future must pay very careful attention to ways and means of bringing our economy into equilibrium and keeping it there.
The government must come to realize that if they are to play their part, the part that government should play in this matter of

bringing and keeping the economy in a condition of equilibrium, the main problem will be that of adjusting purchasing power to production. I think that problem of adjusting purchasing power to production is our most important problem even today. That problem will become even more important tomorrow. I ask hon. members to think what it will be tomorrow with atomic power in industry, with electronics and industrial food production and all the other advances in farming and industry which we are only beginning to realize today. Under these new circumstances of the future the problem of the adjustment of purchasing power may become a matter of life or death for this civilization, rather than just the most important problem that we face. I impress that upon hon. members and recommend it to their study.
It is trite to say that we have solved the production problem which, Mr. Speaker, I point out was at one time by far the most difficult one, both as to toil and as to mental effort. The next step, in my judgment, is much easier. It can be summed up in a single sentence. It is a careful statistical survey and bookkeeping balance of currency and book entry money in relation to the value of production. That is putting it in a nutshell. When it is put that way it seems almost too trivial to deserve serious attention; yet it is of tremendous importance, because without it all the heroic efforts that have been made in the past to achieve our present status of industrial power in this and in some other countries of the world may prove to be of little benefit to mankind.
On the other hand, if we accomplish this balance or adjustment of purchasing power to production, both the national and the international situation will be well under way to effective and just solution. Nationally we shall be able to achieve all the material progress that would be technically possible so that we can continue our advance toward more freedom, harmony and happiness amongst our people. Increased leisure, increased community activity and cultural development will by and by add to our enjoyment and our sense of completeness. Internationally, we would be able to balance imports with exports and get rid of all that incitement of the past to export in excess of imports; to try to get a favourable balance of trade, in other words. This, as hon. members can readily see, will improve our relations with all other people.
As for our less fortunate nations, the ones we are talking about here in connection with the Colombo plan, we shall be able to wait until they can afford to pay in goods and
The Budget-Mr. Low
services without embarrassment or hardship to ourselves in any way, because by using the Social Credit financial proposals the exports can be financed without hurting us in any way. I say the greatest problem that we have to face today is this problem of adjustment of purchasing power so that it is brought into equilibrium with our production.
But if the government are going even to begin to bring our economy into equilibrium in the light of all the facts I have mentioned, including specifically the very heavy burden of fixed charges we now have in the budget, there will have to be a change in their thinking; they will have to lay down for themselves and follow some very scientific ideas. I cannot take the time here to mention many of them, perhaps just one or two. I shall depend on my colleagues to follow up with a careful examination of some of the others which are of tremendous importance. However, for a few moments I should like to deal with one of those ideas which I think the government must attend to, and which I think is very pressing. It has been mentioned to some extent by both the speakers who preceded me today. I refer to ways and means of keeping farm cash income in balance with total factory salaries and wages, and along with that ways of making effective use of the total market that is possible within our country.
Some months ago I was attracted to a short pungent statement by Carl H. Wilken, who is a successful Iowa farmer and a specialist in economic research in the United States. He said:
It is foolish to think we cannot have just as much prosperity in times of peace as in wartime. With the greatest productive system in the world, the American people ought to be smart enough to find out how to keep it working at its full rate. It can be done. All that is necessary is to make use of the total market that is possible in this country. The key to such a prosperity and the total market on which it depends is farm income.
This is the end of Mr. Wilken's quotation. I was attracted to it and I did some research work, gathering as many statistics as I possibly could from the dominion bureau of statistics and from other places, to see if it applied to our own country. In my judgment, we in Canada have neglected this key far too long. It is the key to the total use of our internal market. Farm cash income has been allowed to decline seriously, especially during the past year. This decline has been variously estimated at between $300 and $500 million. Second, farm income has not been able to play its important part in the total Canadian market. Our industrial output has had to be cut off in various lines and serious
2966	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Low
unemployment has resulted, as has been discussed already at length in this house.
So there are good reasons why farm cash income holds what I call a key position in our Canadian economy. A look at the record will reveal this important fact. Under normal peacetime conditions the total national cash farm income runs at an almost exact level with total wages and salaries paid out by the factories of the country. The two hold to an approximate ratio of $1 of farm cash income to $1 of factory payrolls. During the long peace period from 1921 to 1938, whenever farm cash income declined for any reason, factory payrolls had to be adjusted downward to meet it; and when farm income rose factory salaries and wages rose in the same ratio. But there were always very serious shocks to the economy when factory payrolls did have to be adjusted downward to meet a reduced farm cash income.
This balance was upset soon after world war II broke out. Wage costs and industrial employment rose with the great demand for arms while farm prices were held down under price control policies. This landed us into 1944 with an abnormal situation, namely total factory salaries and wages of $2,209,621,370 and total farm income of $1,828,825,000. It will be seen that there was nearly $400,000,000 of a disparity.
Many economists had predicted that we would go into a depression by 1946 after the end of the war, but we did not. Several things prevented it, but none was more important than the restoration of the balance between farm cash income and factory wages and salaries. Farm income rose in 1946 by $150,000,000 to a total of $1,742,440,000; factory payrolls in that year totalled $1,740,000,000 in round figures, a reduction from 1945 of over $100,000,000 because the end of hostilities had cut back our war needs.
This provided a sound foundation for the period of general expansion which followed. The normal dollar for dollar ratio continued through 1947 and 1948. In 1950 farm cash income suffered a decline of $300,000,000 and unemployment was beginning to show itself when the Korean war broke out in the late spring of that year. As a result factory payrolls shot up to the highest levels in our history, reaching $2,771,267,000 for 1950 and $3,276,280,917 for 1951. Again we saw a period of unbalance. When we came to 1954 we saw a tapering off of defence spending, but because farm cash income sagged seriously there was no market in rural areas for the products of the factories; therefore unemployment appeared in very serious proportions. That was in 1954.


At the present time there is an unbalance between farm income and factory payrolls, and that I think is the most critical spot in our whole economy today. When the farmers of the country cannot buy the goods which are being made by the factories the only thing the factories can do is shut down temporarily and turn people out of work. This is a shock to the whole economy. We have to come to realize the vital importance, therefore, of farm cash income to industry and labour. I am convinced that for practical purposes the total dollar income of industry and labour is limited, if not completely determined, by the existing level of farm cash income. I think that is something worth studying by our economists here.
It should be borne in mind that the demand for factory goods that is created by farm cash income is not something that is limited to the farmers alone. An examination of all the facts will show that at least 50 per cent of Canada's total population live in small cities and towns and on land around those towns. Most of those towns and villages are really service centres between the factories and the farms, and they derive their support from farm income almost entirely. That farm cash income is distributed among the dealers and service people in those towns and small cities and villages, and it creates good business everywhere. Competent investigators have found that when a farm dollar starts its course from the farmer who receives it for his product it results in an average of approximately $1 in wages for the factory worker; and in addition-and this is the surprising thing-$7 in national income by the time it completes the full economic circuit that it makes through all the service centres of these towns and villages and small cities. That is a startling fact.
That may give you some idea why farm cash income is the key to the total market that we must have in our country for peacetime prosperity. I am convinced that we can have peacetime prosperity only with farm cash income levels in proper balance with manufactured goods, prices and factory wages. Otherwise we cannot have the total market that industry requires to operate at full capacity and thus to keep our people gainfully employed.
The government must come to realize this, too, and to understand that the key to the use of the total market within Canada is farm cash income.	I point out here that the
most important market that Canada has is its own people; fully 85 per cent of all that we produce is consumed by our own people. That is why we in the Social Credit movement have placed such emphasis upon the

proper use of the home market by urging the government to make certain that this market is constantly supplied with enough purchasing power to buy the goods that Canada produces if it wants them. That is what we mean when we speak of keeping our economy in a state of equilibrium. It should be possible for our people to buy our total production if they want it.
I think the government and businessmen and industrial leaders and the labourers of the country should be just as much concerned as are the farmers in making sure that farm prices and farm income are restored to a parity level as soon as possible. We all have a stake in how much the farmer is able to obtain for his efforts on the farm, because all of us depend upon that basic farm income for our own incomes. When I speak for the farmer, therefore, I am speaking also for the industrial people as well as for ourselves. I think this is the key to our economic situation in Canada. I think also that the general public should be correctly informed about this whole very important matter of farm cash income.
This brings me to my conclusion in connection with this criticism of the budget. As I said before, I think the greatest weakness of the budget is that it has failed to do anything for the farmer, and certainly has failed to take any steps whatsoever to bring the total of farm cash income once more into balance with total factory salaries and wages, something which is absolutely essential if we are to have peacetime prosperity.
We in this group are firm in our belief that the country and the government will have to adopt a well-conceived and comprehensive program of marketing and price supports for agriculture. The adoption of a proper price support program is the only way by which the total of farm cash income can be kept in fair equilibrium with the total of factory salaries and wages in Canada. I know there are many newspaper people and businessmen who today are expressing their opposition to the adoption of farm price supports, and they point to the experience of the United States as a horrible example to deter the Canadian people from going further in their demands for a program of this kind.
But I am going to say that I am convinced that the general public are not being properly informed about farm price supports and the kind of program that can be made to succeed. At the present time most of our people are being told only how much it costs to maintain farm price supports. Some newspapers in the country and other critics are pointing out
The Budget-Mr. Low
that the cost would be too high. In my judgment the cost of agricultural support prices would be far less than the cost of widespread unemployment, and farm price supports would be effective in keeping a balance and equilibrium in our economy. I am convinced that some such price support program as was recently suggested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture would be of tremendous help in doing the kind of job that must be done if we are to have this peacetime prosperity of which I have spoken on several occasions.
I think we should do everything we can to help our people understand what happens when farm income is kept at a reasonable level; that is, how it increases factory payrolls and opportunities for a higher standard of living for all Canadians. Let us sincerely hope that the Minister of Finance and the government will, in the next few months, make a thorough study of the possibilities in this proposal of a system of price supports for agriculture, and that they will soon thereafter-at least by the next budget-come prepared to lay before parliament a price support program that will do the kind of job that must be done if purchasing power is to be adjusted to equal our production. We know this system can help to do the job.
But I warn the government that they will have to have a change in thinking. Unless they pull those dollar signs off their eyes and begin to see the realities beneath the dollar signs they will never be able to adopt the kind of policies that will help us to make use of the total market available in this country. They will have to adopt some better financial proposals as well, and we recommend to them the proposals which Social Crediters have been making over the years as a means of bringing our economy into equilibrium and keeping it there.
Mr. Speaker, in closing I repeat that the adjustment of purchasing power to production is the most important problem facing the Canadian people today. It is the answer to the economic problem, and I say there is no question in our minds about that matter at the present time.
I should like to be able to deal with other phases of the budget but time will not permit me to do so. I should like to have said something about the royal commission. That is exactly the kind of thing we have been proposing for the last 15 years in this house. Certainly ever since I came here in 1945 my colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and others have been pleading with the government to appoint a royal commission to examine into all phases of our economic activity and bring in proposals that

The Budget-Mr. Balcom will help us to achieve the high standard of living that we can achieve in this great country, to make the wisest possible use of our economic possibilities, and particularly to keep our economy in a state of equilibrium. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard, in this house and outside of it, a great many speeches about this great country of ours. We congratulate ourselves on our great size, our natural resources, our hydro power and other physical assets. But I suggest that our greatest asset is stable government. Great wealth is of little value to the world, and of not much satisfaction to ourselves, unless it is properly used. In his first budget the Minister of Finance has shown his acceptance of responsibility and has maintained the high tradition of courage and progressive action so vital to our continued growth.
At the outset I should like to commend the tariff changes contained in the budget which will be of benefit to our farmers. Of particular interest to Nova Scotia, where the poultry industry has grown by leaps and bounds, is the reduction or elimination of tariffs on poultry eviscerating equipment. Similar assistance is afforded to the fisheries in the reduction of duty on fish meal plant and fish cooking equipment. Also of interest is the elimination of duty on fishing vessels over 100 feet in length.
It would be even more satisfactory if, by action in this house, we could reduce the duty on our fish entering the United States market. That is, to be sure, something that is outside our power, but there is a problem on which action could be taken.
1 refer to the restriction on trawlers operating off the shores of Nova Scotia. By international agreement United States trawlers can come within three miles of the coast, but our Canadian trawlers must stay outside the 12-mile limit. The obvious solution is, perhaps, to change the law respecting Canadian trawlers, but there are several objections to this course. The government has recognized the interests of the inshore fishermen in the recently announced restriction on trawlers inside the famous St. Margarets bay. Furthermore, in the interests of conservation the 12-mile limit may be the more desirable.
Would it, Mr. Speaker, be possible to have this problem reviewed by the northwest Atlantic fisheries council? Its primary purpose is conservation, and it has had marked success in obtaining regulation of the fisheries


off the New England coast. It may be that the United States industry would respond to a proposal from the council which was based on a sound conservation policy. Our objective might then be accomplished without furnishing ammunition for higher tariffs on our fish products entering the United States market.
Apart from tax and tariff matters, there is in the budget speech a great deal that is of importance to all Canadians. As a Nova Scotian I was most interested in the minister's remarks on dominion-provincial relations, particularly the references to the tax rental agreements. I find it rather difficult to become greatly concerned over whether or not we achieve formal reallocation of financial powers and responsibilities as between the dominion and the provinces for, as the minister has said, it is not easy to visualize an arrangement which will meet all future contingencies.
The division of powers and responsibilities established by the British North America Act was practical for many years after 1867. After the turn of the century the rapid geographic expansion and the industrial development, proceeding at vastly different rates in different areas, changed the face of this country, but our constitution remained as it was in 1867.
Then came the depression of the thirties, under the stress of which our federal system began cracking at the seams. As in the maritime provinces, the obvious weaknesses which appeared in the thirties were only the exaggerated symptoms of unhealthy conditions which had existed for a quarter of a century. They were only soothed, not cured, by subsidy arrangements such as, for example, the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and so on.
The tax rental approach, while not without disadvantages, has brought substantial benefits to all the people of Canada and the various provincial governments. That the proportionate advantage varies among the provinces goes without saying, for otherwise such agreements would be unnecessary. I want to illustrate my point with some figures.
The federal tax rental agreements provide varying proportions of the revenue of the provinces. These proportions ranged from 22 per cent for Alberta to 47 per cent for Manitoba in 1953. In that year the proportion for Nova Scotia was 39 per cent. In this comparison we therefore find ourselves in the upper brackets but the advantage, I fear, is illusory. Such a comparison does not take into account the number, variety, and cost of services which may vary from one province to another. It does indicate, however, the importance to our revenue picture

of the federal grants. The withdrawal of these funds would create serious problems in the provinces with a small tax base. In the event of a return to pre-war arrangements we in Nova Scotia would be faced with a prohibitive tax level or a reversion to inadequate or substandard services.
That is why I was so heartened by the tenor of the minister's remarks on this subject. Some members may disagree with the details or even the methods of approach, but I doubt if anyone would stand in his place and deny the validity of the objective of these agreements, which was stated so aptly by the minister on another occasion when he said:
That objective is to make it financially possible for all the provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions themselves, and to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation.
I believe, and many Nova Scotians agree with me, that this objective can be attained without threatening our provincial autonomy. Indeed, this could easily become a meaningless shibboleth without some measure of redistribution of the wealth which has been accumulated in part at least on the basis of a national market. I am reminded here that "the law, in the majesty of its equality, forbids rich and poor alike to sleep on park benches."
My interest in the varying economic positions of the provinces is not confined to taxation problems. The announcement of the intention to appoint a royal commission to examine Canada's long-term economic problems is welcome. The outline of this proposal indicated a very broad approach, including a study of our productive capacities as well as our external markets. It will include an examination of our population growth in both its regional and age distribution aspects. In his speech the minister said, as found at page 2740 of Hansard of April 5:
X am sure our provincial and municipal governments, our businessmen and producers, management and workers, would like to have comprehensive and carefully documented analyses of our various potentialities.
To that I say "hear, hear". I would add that I hope the regional analysis will not be confined to population studies but will extend to the relative economic positions of the various regions. Specifically, could the minister have the commission examine the possible value of having an agency of the federal government perform services for the Atlantic region similar to those provided by the Federal Reserve Bank in Boston for the New England states?
As I said before, we in the House of Commons should do more than work for the 50433-188
The Budget-Mr. Balcom redistribution of national wealth through tax agreements. We must also work on the more positive line of reducing the economic gap between the provinces. The first step in such a procedure is to know just where we stand, and a thorough-going report on our economic prospects is just such a first step. I would go further, however, and say that a continuing scrutiny is necessary, particularly in the region where both chronic and shortterm problems are the most serious.
Related to the general problem of dominion-provincial relations, Mr. Speaker, is the matter of federal grants to universities. I trust hon. members will bear with me, for they have heard me before, and others as well, urging a more equitable method of distributing these grants among the universities. I make no apology for raising this question again because I feel there has been ample time to correct the very obvious shortcomings of the present arrangement. With the permission of the house I shall quote the per student payment in each province provided for in the 1954-55 estimates. British Columbia receives per student $105.41; Manitoba, $99.26; New Brunswick, $122.59; Alberta, $157.57; Saskatchewan, $162.96; Ontario, $140.98; Prince Edward Island, $214.29; Newfoundland, $394.06, and Nova Scotia, $85.23.
The distribution of the money on the basis of population instead of at a per student rate has the effect of penalizing the province with the highest proportion of students in relation to population. The royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences in recommending financial assistance stressed the importance of the universities in the life of Canada. Because their service is national in scope rather than regional, the commission recommended that the universities receive support from the federal treasury. In the light of this, would it not be more logical for the government to set a uniform national rate per student, irrespective of the location of the university, rather than the present system? In the post-war training of service personnel the Department of Veterans Affairs was able to administer such a scheme without any undue criticism of federal interference in university affairs.
An alternative suggestion is to deal with the professional schools separately and I think the suggestion merits immediate action. I am told that the conference of Canadian universities, in its brief to the commission, assumed that all universities doing the same kind of work would receive the same rate of assistance and proposed a per capita grant ranging from $150 to $200 per student registered in professional faculties, and a single

The Budget-Mr. Balcom grant of $100 per student in other faculties. This was a recognition of the higher costs in particular faculties.
In Nova Scotia we have a university with professional faculties in medicine, dentistry and pharmacy serving the four Atlantic provinces. This means that much of our student body comes from the other Atlantic provinces as well as from farther afield, and of course we welcome them all to Nova Scotia. I think all members will agree that a single institution in these fields for that area is the most desirable set-up. Yet the concentration of students in these professional faculties at Dalhousie has the effect of reducing the financial assistance going to all universities in the province of Nova Scotia.
In this connection will you please note the following figures showing the cost of these professional faculties to the university. The proportion of the operating costs borne by student fee, not including capital charges, for arts and science is 44 per cent, for medicine 23 per cent and for dentistry 33 per cent. The balance has to come out of endowments, gifts or grants. It is true that we must recognize the differing outlooks among the components of our nation. I would be the last person to advocate the promotion of the mass mind or putting a premium on uniformity among our people. Let us accept the fact that we must be oversensitive as to provincial jurisdiction over education. But could we not separate financial assistance for professional training and put that on a per student basis? Then the assistance to the arts and science faculties, which are the heart of any university, would be distributed on a more equitable basis.
Before leaving this subject I should like to have it distinctly understood that we are not suggesting for a moment that the grants to other provinces be reduced. Students in all professional schools could be put on the same special per student rate. The grant for straight university education could then be on a per capita basis with more equitable results.
A tariff change which I feel sure will commend wide support is the elimination of duties on the articles and materials designed for the training of mentally retarded children. This is in line with the constructive policy of rehabilitation which is part of our program for assistance to the disabled. It is very gratifying that efforts are being made to round out that program. Now that allowances are being paid experience has shown some shortcomings, and I should like to urge that immediate consideration be given to the carrying out of the spirit of the act in a sympathetic and understanding fashion.


The Canadian Welfare Council, which appreciates the difficulty in administering and carrying out the provisions of Bill No. 462, made several essential suggestions in their brief to the Prime Minister in May, 1954. If more of these suggestions had been incorporated in our act I believe that we might not now have so many misunderstandings in the provinces. Unfortunately there are people thoughtless and cruel enough to take political advantage of the disabled and handicapped by telling the latter that they are entitled to full pension as disabled persons, at the same time knowing full well that such persons could not qualify under the act. Perhaps in many cases this was done through ignorance or inability to recognize the distinction between "disability" and "handicap".
Total disability can be determined on medical evidence and is so determined for war pensions and workmen's compensation. However, the handicap resulting from a disability is more difficult to ascertain. Total handicap is generally accepted as "unemployable", and unemployability is dependent on many factors such as physical and mental condition, personality, education and training. It is dependent in addition upon the economic and employment possibilities in the locality, plus the attitude of the public and the availability of rehabilitation services.
At this juncture I should like to point out to the minister that in Nova Scotia we have not the variety of jobs for disabled and handicapped persons that are so often readily available in industrial centres. Some applicants should, therefore, be, considered eligible for the pension if suitable work is not available near at hand. A danger stressed in the Canadian Welfare Council brief was the fact that allowances for total or permanent disability, divorced from rehabilitation services, should be granted only when it is definitely proven a person cannot profit from rehabilitation.
Before leaving this subject, Mr. Speaker, I should like to respectfully and humbly suggest to the minister, a man who has a full understanding and appreciation of the dependent position of the disabled and untrained handicapped person, that after a full year of operation the act and regulations be given a complete overhauling. In the meantime I suggest, (1) that no applicant be turned down without being personally interviewed by the medical board; (2) that provision be made for an appeal from the finding of the medical board; this would give the applicant the same right as an applicant for old age assistance or a war veterans pension; (3) that consideration be given to classifying as permanently disabled those patients with arrested tuberculosis who, while living at

home and able to care for personal needs, are unable to perform any kind of work and are dependent on their family; (4) that paraplegics able to stand only with the help of braces or crutches be considered as qualifying for this pension.
These suggestions, and I have more, are given constructively in the hope that the disabled program may be broadened and that disability allowances will be made part of a comprehensive plan providing for the economic needs of all disabled persons, as recommended by the Canadian Welfare Council.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore in this instance. He is quite right when he says that in his many years here it has always been understood that one could discuss almost any subject in the budget debate. If the hon. member says that, because he needs more time, he is going to discuss that subject now and pursue it further on Thursday, would not his action defeat the purpose of standing order 37 which says that every hon. member is entitled to speak for 40 minutes on any one topic? Would it not also defeat the other rule as set out in standing order 43, which says that a member cannot speak twice to any question?
So there we are. The hon. member may speak for only 40 minutes, and he is not permitted to speak twice. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The speech from the throne. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is reported on page 825 of Hansard of February 3, 1955, as having asked me why I did not tell the people about Alberta defaulting her bonds. I am not using his words, so the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar can be at ease. Later on he again asked me why I did not tell why Alberta had defaulted her bonds. Again I am not using his words. I propose now to tell about Alberta's so-called defaulting of bonds.
I said on a previous occasion that Alberta had no alternative. Alberta did not default on her bonds, she was forced into default by a series of circumstances which I now intend to present to the house. In doing so I think I am perfectly in order in this budget debate.
Let us recall that as of March 31, 1936, Alberta owed $167,037,144 carrying an average interest rate of 4 [DOT] 95 per cent. The annual revenue which Alberta was able to gather was only $15,000,000, so about 49 cents out of every revenue dollar had to be used to pay interest on the debt. I think today anyone will realize that a province like Alberta would have serious difficulty giving anything like the services to which the people were entitled with just slightly more than half of $15,000,000, and at the same time pay the cost of government.
This provincial debt had been contracted during years of relative prosperity, considering the prices for goods which were then prevailing. That was when much of the debt was contracted, except what was contracted during the depression in respect of relief. As I say, it was contracted when prices were fairly good and there was a measure of prosperity.
Up to that time Alberta had been largely an agricultural community. Agricultural prices were very low when Social Credit
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore came in. Let us get the picture clearly. In large measure the debt had been contracted while times were relatively good, we will say in the twenties and in the years preceding the twenties, from 1905 on. During that time prices were fairly high. Then prices went away down to an all-time low. Conditions were such that it was next to impossible for farmers to pay their taxes.
Under those circumstances the Social Credit government was called upon to service a debt which had been contracted at a time of high prices for agricultural products and to do so with revenues which were being collected from farmers when prices were very low. This is the first important thing for everybody to get straight who wishes to understand the defaulting on Alberta's debt, or at least the so-called defaulting.
The master question that had to be answered when William Aberhart took office in 1935 was this: Could the Alberta economy at that time, in the depression, carry $167 million of debt at an average interest rate of 4-95 per cent? Premier Aberhart seriously doubted that it could. Premier Aberhart therefore employed R. J. Magor of Montreal, the best expert he could learn of, to come to Edmonton to examine into every pertinent fact with regard to Alberta's economy, particularly having reference to the people's capacity to pay taxes and the government's consequent capacity to pay interest and at the same time provide its people with the reasonable minimum standard of services.
After a thorough study Mr. Magor presented a comprehensive report. I am glad that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) is here beside me. He was at that time in the legislature, and shortly thereafter, if not up to that time, had been charged with the responsibility of acting as provincial treasurer.
As I was saying, after a thoroughgoing study Mr. Magor submitted a comprehensive report in which he gave it as his opinion that Alberta simply could not pay 4-95 per cent on $167 million of debt. Let it be borne in mind that under the U.F.A. government which held office between 1921 and 1935 the province had incurred a debt of $10 million in the form of what were called Alberta savings certificates. An Alberta savings certificate was a demand promissory note bearing interest at 4 per cent.
So that people out in the country who may read this speech and who may not have the ability to comprehend that the members of this house would have, may I make this explanation. If a citizen had $100 and felt that he would like to put it on deposit at 4 per cent interest, he could go to the appropriate officials of the Alberta government,

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore turn in the $100 and obtain from the officials of Alberta a promise to pay, bearing interest at 4 per cent; that was a promise which the province agreed to make good on demand. In other words the individual could deposit his $100, obtain his certificate, leave his $100 there for six weeks, or six days, then go and demand his $100 and the province had to give him back his $100, no matter in what condition the province happened to find itself. Such was the Alberta savings certificate debt.
Hon. members will realize that with $10 million of indebtedness in the form of Alberta savings certificates, any provincial government whatsoever would have been in an extremely vulnerable position in case any considerable number of people holding these certificates should come and ask for their money at one time, especially if there was no reserve to take care of such a contingency. This is the first all-important thing to be borne in mind.
The next one is this. Let it be borne in mind that the inability to service these demand certificates had, on August 27, 1935, precipitated Alberta into the loss of her credit at least five days before the Social Credit party took office on September 3. All those who have any desire to be fair in appraising Alberta must bear this fact in mind. Considerable propaganda was circulated all over the country, much of it just downright lies, which purported to blame the Social Credit administration for the loss of Alberta's credit. It was all completely fallacious. The inability to service these savings certificates had caused the province to lose its credit, technically, five days before the Social Credit administration took office, although five days after the election. Let us remember that the election was on August 22, 1935, but the inability to service-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Please get this exactly
straight. The government was elected on August 22, 1935. Technically the U.F.A. government, which was still in office on August 27, had to default on these savings certificates. This was five days before the Social Credit government took office. So no blame could possibly be attached to the Social Credit government for the defaulting on Alberta's savings certificate debt.
The hon. member for Peace River reminds me that the previous government, that is the U.F.A. government, had left no reserve whatsoever. I do not want to be too harsh on the previous government. I have no particular complaint against the U.F.A. government which preceded the Social Credit government, because that government was obliged


to take Alberta through the terrible depression years in which the costs of relief and other expenses were so great that they were forced into a tremendous increase of debt, a thing which they did not in any way desire to be forced into. However, those were the circumstances.
I think probably what I have already said is enough to show the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that, on the score of defaulting on Alberta's debt, he has an extremely poor case against Social Credit, and no honourable man would press that case. I hope he is honourable enough to go out all over the country and tell the absolute truth. Then everybody will be much happier.
Because of the things I have already mentioned, it was impossible for Alberta to borrow in the world's money markets. Just as soon as the province technically defaulted on August 27 it no longer could go into the world's markets and borrow money. This is an extremely important fact. But this one also is important. The U.F.A. government had been unable to borrow money on the world's markets since the early spring of 1935; it seems to me it was some time in April. Premier Reid, who was then acting premier of the province, came to Ottawa endeavouring to get $750,000-I can remember quite distinctly reading about it-and found himself unable to get a cent. This fact is extremely important. It indicates that the province of Alberta had been really forced into default months before the Social Credit government was elected or took office.
Unfortunately malicious, adverse propaganda all over North America had so poisoned people against Aberhart and Alberta that conditions had been rendered extraordinarily and most unjustly difficult. It is important for people who did not live through those days to know that there was an outburst of adverse comment and criticism all over the country closely resembling the kind of thing that has burst out against Chiang Kai-shek, and engineered by the selfsame people.
Political opposition to Social Credit made it impossible for Alberta to borrow from the federal government of Canada. The prime minister in those days, the late William Lyon Mackenzie King, before the election was quite enthusiastic in his remarks about hands off Alberta. But just as soon as he got in power he had hands on Alberta, restraining her in every move. In addition the Bank of Canada failed to come to the aid of the province, though shortly afterward they did recommend substantial help to both Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

I hope the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys tells everybody about that. That is important. When a province like Alberta, no matter what the government is, goes to the Bank of Canada for assistance after she has done her part the very best she could and is denied assistance, it constitutes a scandal against the Bank of Canada. I wish the minister were here. However, I am sure he will read what I am saying and I hope his friends will point it out to him. I should like to ask him to tell the house some time what his solution for the problem would have been, what he would have done if he had been in Mr. Aberhart's position as premier of Alberta. And I hope he will take the trouble to document what he tells us so we shall have some evidence that he knows what he is talking about.
This was the situation. Premier Aberhart was positive that a rate of 4'95 per cent was too high and could not be borne. The bondholders and dealers in Toronto, Montreal and New York could not possibly understand the economic problem in Alberta. They could not see how it could be that if a farmer contracted a debt of $1,500, let us say, with wheat at $1.50 a bushel, and then when the time came to repay the debt found wheat was down to 25 cents a bushel, there would inevitably be reasons why the farmer could not pay the debt. It seemed impossible to make them understand that.
The bondholders hoped and believed that Premier Aberhart could and would be defeated in the 1940 election. They were not a bit desirous of being fair. But what did Aberhart do? He communicated with Alberta's bondholders asking them to refund Alberta's debt at a rate possible for Alberta to bear. In a general way he put the case to them much like this. Now, we know we owe you a good deal of money, but this administration does not owe it. In the legislature of Alberta there is not one single man who was there when the debt was contracted. They are not in any way to blame. We are desirous of being honourable with the bondholders, but it is simply idle for us to go on trying to pay an interest rate which we cannot pay, thereby accumulating more and more debt until we get to the point where you will lose everything you have invested in Alberta. We suggest that you be fair about this matter and agree to an interest rate we can carry. We will then pay the interest rate and we will pay off the bonds.
That was something like the proposition he offered them, but the bondholders paid little heed to Aberhart's request. The bondholders sent into Alberta a team of experts to study the situation and report. In this team the key 50433-189
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore man was Courtland Elliott. I do not wish to suggest anything against Courtland Elliott. As far as I know he is a very honourable and capable man. This team believed its findings had proved that Alberta could pay 5 per cent. The bondholders therefore sternly refused to refund Alberta's debt at a lower interest rate. Alberta then offered the bondholders one-half of the interest rate then carried by her bonds, pending further efforts to convince them that the cut was justified. The bondholders forthwith declared Alberta to be in default on her bonds.
Let me pause a minute to restate the situation so hon. members can understand just what happened. Alberta had been pointing out to the bondholders that she simply could not carry this heavy rate of interest, and finally she got to the point where she offered them one-half of the interest rate, whereupon they immediately declared her bonds in default. Probably when the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys gets around to the subject he will justify the action of the bondholders in doing that, and will explain how in the world under circumstances like that he can honestly say that Alberta defaulted on her bonds.
It looks as though we are going to have the filthiest election in the history of Canada, judging by the way the Liberals are behaving in Alberta and British Columbia. I think, therefore, it is fitting that we should warn ourselves beforehand that there is not going to be very much honour on one side in the coming election. Let us get the facts straight, and I do hope there will be enough Liberals who will tell the truth about the whole matter so as to keep it from being misrepresented. I am giving them the opportunity to do so by putting the facts on the record, with the man who was provincial treasurer during those trying times, the hon. member for Peace River, sitting right beside me.
The Alberta government announced that the government itself had cut the interest rate by one-half on all outstanding bonds. That was not defaulting by any means. That was simply refusing to pay a heavy rate of interest in consideration of the fact that the prices of everything Alberta was producing and marketing had fallen to such a low level as to render it impossible for her to carry out her commitments previously made.
Let it be borne in mind that the fall in prices had resulted not from Alberta's action, but had resulted, if it resulted from anything, from the actions of men in Ottawa and in the United States who represented the very governments with which Alberta was dealing. We have gotten away from those

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore terrible times now and are able to look back, and we know that the depression with which we were struggling in 1935 was brought on directly by the United States of America and spread its devastating effect all over the world. Then we had bondholders in the United States of America and their friends in Canada blaming Alberta because she had been so sorely hit by a depression which was engineered and put into operation in the United States.
Now we come to what was to be done about this defaulting. If Alberta had left the situation just as it was without undertaking to do anything it would have been a different matter, but she was desirous of doing what was right. The hon. member for Peace River, then the provincial treasurer of Alberta, who is here to testify if I err in any way, in the spring of 1938 set about for the provincial government to recover Alberta's credit, and the province was behind him fully. He administered the treasurer's department for the provincial government with the utmost care, skill and economy. That was all he could do. He organized the government's financial affairs with the strictest wisdom. In fact, I think one of the greatest things he has ever done was that very job he did then.
He husbanded every dollar with the utmost frugality and used it with the utmost wisdom, dealing equitably with the Alberta savings certificates problem and with preparations for possible refunding. He put away a little bit here and there, at the same time trying to take care of those who were suffering, quite unintentionally, because they were unable to get the money they had lent the government in return for Alberta savings certificates. He paid off a part of the debt each year.
I hope the Liberal enthusiasts who go all over western Canada will remember to tell that Social Credit Alberta started to pay off the debt immediately. It was not because of oil that she started to pay off the debt. The large discoveries of oil did not occur until 1947. Alberta had made great progress in reducing her debt by that time, showing that she was getting herself on her feet and would have done so probably without the oil, although it would certainly have taken much longer.
The provincial treasurer then set out to visit the bondholders and others personally. He sought and obtained an appointment with the bondholders' protective council. It was adamant. It would not even listen to him, much to its disgrace. He then went to Ottawa and conferred with Dr. Clark, the deputy


minister of finance, first to enlist Ottawa official's support in his refunding project, and second to ask that the dominion scale down the $8 million of treasury bills Alberta owed Ottawa. Either one of those things could have been done, but Dr. Clark was much more adamant.
He asked also that Alberta be given the royal commission's natural resources award, which would have amounted to over $10 million. This was a sum that was really coming to Alberta. It was compensation for the amount of money that Alberta had not been able to obtain during the many years Ottawa maintained control of and administered Alberta's resources. Ottawa controlled these resources from 1905, when Alberta became a province, until 1932 when they were finally handed over to Alberta.
Now, that $10 million could have been advanced to Alberta and would have enabled Alberta to deal completely with the savings certificate problem and, technically, to restore her credit. However, this $10 million was refused. He went to Montreal, Toronto, New York, Chicago and Los Angeles to confer with the bondholders and try to convince them that they should negotiate with Alberta. Among those he visited were the Kuhn, Loeb Company, Brown, Harriman and Company, the Mayflower Association, Wood, Gundy and Company, and Dominion Securities. Everywhere he found it almost impossible to make men believe-in most cases even to listen- that any Social Credit official could be sincere and honourable. This illustrates how far the lying propaganda had gone. He got nowhere.

Very likely, but I would rather be in his position than in yours.
Finally he decided to talk with Courtland Elliott, the man who had assured the bondholders that Alberta could pay 5 per cent on her bonds. Mr. Low obtained an audience with that key man and prevailed upon Courtland Elliott to go over the various conclusions Mr. Elliott had arrived at which had satisfied him that Alberta could stand 5 per cent. He got Mr. Elliott to examine and talk over with him the evidence upon which Mr. Elliott had based his conclusions. They went into the details concerning the many elements that combine to make up Alberta's highly complex economy as they are set out in a very fine book called "The Case for Alberta" which Mr. Low was largely instrumental in having prepared in preparation for the Rowell-Sirois conference on dominion-provincial relations.
Gradually Courtland Elliott apparently came to see-it is impossible to tell exactly-that

probably certain things had been overlooked and it would be reasonable to review the whole situation in respect of the amount that Alberta could pay. At length he apparently saw that Alberta had a real case, one that any honest man must allow. Mr. Elliott became a supporter of Alberta's case, much to his credit. Apparently Mr. Low with Mr. Elliott's help convinced Mr. John Hope, a representative of Dominion Securities, and Dominion Securities moved in behind Alberta, much to its honour and credit. Wood, Gundy and Company followed, and those two Canadian companies brought the United States companies into understanding sympathy with Alberta's refunding program, which was finally accomplished on an average coupon rate of 2-78 per cent. Alberta's credit was restored, both at home and abroad.
Probably I have gone far enough and said all that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys desired me to say. There is much more that I could say, but I think probably I have said sufficient on this occasion concerning this matter, which is very important.
It is important for another reason, Mr. Speaker. Every member, except two, who sits in this house comes from some province. Each of those provinces is having great difficulty in dealing with its financial affairs. If there is any man in this house who thinks that is not the case, I suggest he obtain permission to attend the dominion-provincial conference which is to convene before very long, and he will very soon find out. There is not a province in this dominion that is not in a relatively vulnerable position financially.

Ontario, too. I was here during the depression, and I heard sad tales about the way people were being treated in various Ontario cities and towns. They are beginning to suffer now in Ontario cities and towns. If the unemployment problem gets three times worse the strain that will be placed on Ontario will be unbearable, even with Ontario's wealth. Especially will this be so if the agricultural income referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River does not increase. Then the factories in Ontario will find themselves unable to sell enough of their goods to make their industries pay. They will be in serious difficulty.
Even if Ontario should not be in this difficulty, that is no reason why Saskatchewan, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and at least three-quarters of the provinces of this dominion might not be in an impossible position within a year. Let us bear that in mind. They will be in that position, not 50433-189J
The Budget-Mr. Rowe because of any measures taken by them but because of measures taken right here in Ottawa. No one is blaming the provinces today for the unemployment problem. The unemployment problem developing today is a result of the policies adopted right in Ottawa in this house. Let us bear that in mind. Remember that any province, put into a sufficient number of difficulties, ultimately will be forced to default its bonds or to put its people under circumstances which no civilized people ought to endure.
Now, Alberta was just one example. She was hit harder, and there were three or four reasons why she was hit harder. In the first place, Alberta paid a higher railway rate on everything she bought coming from the east than any other province in Canada. She paid more on goods she shipped east and west than any other province in Canada. In addition to that, Alberta was in the Palliser triangle and consequently she had to deal with droughts, seed grain relief and all that sort of thing. Only two other provinces had anything like that. Another thing was that when the land was given to the Hudson's Bay Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway, to compensate them for certain considerations in the west, that land was taken out of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was taken in such a way that the population of Alberta has had to spread out over a wide area, making the costs of roads, schools and telephones greater than they should have been.
These were just a few of the difficulties under which Alberta laboured. I think probably I have said as much as is necessary at the present time. But I would just tell the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys that any time he wants to enter into a further discussion of this matter, all he needs to do is let me know, and I shall be right here.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the budget speech this year as I have on many other occasions. One has to search his imagination in order to understand what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) had in mind. The hon. member who replied this afternoon for the official opposition said that it confused him, and I am sure it has confused many people in this country.
It seems strange, after so many years of sin-pluses, so many years when we were told that we should not reduce taxation even though we were not spending as much as we were collecting, that now, at a time when we are spending more than we are collecting, we are told that we should collect less. This is not in keeping with the Scottish instincts of the Minister of Finance. It seems to me that in delivering this budget he either

The Budget-Mr. Rowe had a subtle inclination to popularize himself throughout the country, or else he was copying what someone else had done; because it does not sound like him at all.
Coming from almost the same district in Ontario as the minister, and he and I having had to struggle during our lives for our very existence in that district, I cannot help thinking that he must have had some other idea in mind.
I do not know whether this is a cyclical budget or a sickening budget, or just what type of budget it is. Someone intimated this afternoon to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) that it might be a cyclical budget. He spoke with that dry, Scottish humour of his; and those of you who do not like him, simply because you belong to the other side of politics, would do well to read his speech tomorrow, where he pointed out the inconsistencies of the Liberal party in the last number of years. I am sure if hon. members will read that speech they will realize that even the hon. member for Greenwood, with his enlightened mind, was still confused. He did mention, however, that it might have been a speech that was not intended to solve the economic problems of the country, but rather that it might have been one intended to solve the political problem of the Minister of Finance himself who, I see, shakes his head.
