subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened to Liberal apostles for the last 30 years in this house. They do not disturb me for a moment, Mr. Speaker. I say again you will hear it in Renfrew; you will hear it in Lanark, and you will hear it down through the Ottawa valley. You will hear it down in Cornwall and along the St. Lawrence valley. You will hear it in every industrial riding in Canada and in the agricultural ridings. You will hear the rumblings in the mulberry bushes. My friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) has quite a few unemployed in his riding.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, there were 800 fewer unemployed in Fort William last week than there were a year ago. That is from a source that does not tell a lie.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, but there were many unemployed last year and more expecting to go on strike this year. 1 tell the hon. member for Fort William that I know something about the Fort William district, and I shall have something to say to him a little later on. I am not going to enlarge upon that. If there are 800 fewer unemployed I am sure the hon. member can tell me that there are still several thousand unemployed at the head of the lakes, which is a small part of Canada.
My, how this government boasts. It boasts of a country with such resources that no similar number of people in the world has ever enjoyed. It boasts about the $300 million railroad into Labrador to bring out the iron ore in that district. It boasts of the Kitimat development and the development of the resources up there. It boasts of a prairie land that is richer than land which any other people in the world enjoy. It boasts that no other 14 million people in the world have ever had the resources that we have at hand. Yet it says in one small district there are 800 fewer unemployed now than there were, but several thousands are still unemployed. We now have more people unemployed than any other important country in the world.
Stop and think of it, Mr. Speaker. What is wrong? We have a government that has sat idly by. It has been in power so long that it has become sleepy at the switch. As this budget indicates and as the Minister of Finance suggests, now that we are spending more than we collect we are going to start to collect less. When we were spending less

The Budget-Mr. Rowe than we collected, we collected more. Is it cyclical budgeting? I am not sure what the term is. If I were not in parliament I could give it a term.
The Minister of Finance laughs. He himself does not have a description for it. What is the plan of this government? They have no fiscal policy; they have no immigration policy; they have no financial policy. Why do we have a gunshot prescription along the line of reduction in taxes which means so little, as was exemplified by speakers who preceded me today? Is our development sound today? Ask the farmer. My hon. friend might ask the farmers of Renfrew county. Perhaps he has not met many of them for some time. He might ask them if they think the dairy industry is healthy; he might ask them if the poultry and egg industry is healthy; he might ask them if the beef cattle industry is healthy. There is nothing in this budget that will help the farmer.
I was amazed that the Minister of National Revenue would even venture to challenge the argument that the textile industry of this country is not in a healthy condition today. Surely no one who has worshipped at the shrine of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier as he has, can now say that our textile industry is flourishing. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier fashioned the policy of those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, a policy that half of them have never followed since because we have more mongrel stripes of fiscal policy across there than have ever been in one group since confederation. We have the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) who is a higher protectionist than the highest protectionist on this side. We have some hon. gentlemen in the other corner in the house who are lower protectionists than the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier ever proposed to be, and we have those in the centre who do not say where they are going because they do not know. The ones on the left of Mr. Speaker have no fiscal policy whatsoever.
I wonder whether they ever pause to wonder, if it were not for the expenditure on defence, if it were not for the expenditure on expansion of industries that hope they will get a square deal in this country later on, what would happen to our development at the present time? Does the Minister of Finance not pause to realize that Canada with 14 million people imports more finished products representing the labour of foreign countries than the United States with 160 million people? We import more in actual dollars, not percentage-wise, than the United States. I would ask my hon. friend to take off that old dusty halo of free trade which is around his head and look the issues 

squarely in the eye and realize that if we are to expand industry we must find a home market in this country.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, proposes to reduce corporation taxes by some 2 per cent. That may help a little bit. I am one of those who believe that if you give corporations a chance they will give employment. If you increase depreciation, they will do their part. I do not agree with some of my friends to my immediate left. I am not sure at times where my friends to my extreme left are going. My friends to my immediate left suggest that all these things should be taken over by the government. I wonder who would be left to pay the taxes.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that when you tax corporations you tax the shareholders of the corporations and you tax all along the line. You milk industry of most of the incentive that gives employment to greater numbers; therefore I am bound to agree with the Minister of Finance in his slight, modest gesture to encourage industry by reducing corporation taxes by 2 per cent. You are still taking almost half of everything the corporation makes. The Minister of Finance, or his colleagues, are criticizing industry for not running their business right. They say we need more efficiency in order to pay more wages. I do not know any machinery that needs more efficiency than the cabinet right there in the front row.
Independent of politics, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that they employ-and I shall vote for it-an efficiency expert and pay him far more than any of the present cabinet is worth to show them the fallacy of some of their politics.

I am afraid if I did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre might doubt my motives. I think if the hon. member wanted to please a lot of people he might have reduced the sales tax. I can remember the late Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King almost weeping in this house when he ridiculed the Conservative party for putting on a 6 per cent sales tax. He said that it was the most iniquitous tax ever imposed on the people of any country. The poor pensioners, the war widows, the veterans and the crippled people would have to pay 6 per cent on everything they bought. He was going to remove it immediately; he threatened to remove it, but he got into power and added 2 per cent more, and we are now paying about 10 per cent. These apostles of economy now suggest that they have reduced the income tax for those who pay income tax, but the sales tax stays as it was.
It seems to me that is a strange type of procedure. If the Minister of Finance had said that things look a little dangerous, that there was a chance that the $26 billion revenue would be reduced to $22 billion; if he had said as he said in Montreal that taxes are too high-the minister shakes his head, indicating that he did not say that.

speechtext:
He heard you use the words, but from what he said this afternoon I thought those were the words you used. That statement seems to be just as mysterious as the budget itself. I shall not enlarge on that further. I say again that the budget is a most difficult document to understand. After listening to the Minister of Finance I am convinced that this government has no definite and fixed policy. The Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, formerly prime minister of this country, stated in 1919 that they had what was more or less a chart. It was just like the chart you use when you go to sea. If there is a storm you forget the chart. He forgot it shortly after he was elected. He never followed the chart. The present government have not even a chart. They are drifting on the ebb and flow of good times.
For ten years this government have drifted on the crest of a prosperity which was more or less abnormal and unnatural. They have no policy with respect to fiscal matters; they have no fixed policy with respect to taxation; they have no fixed policy with reference to the development of our resources for our own people. I shall not go into that tonight in detail, but I say that no government since confederation has been so lucky. We are a people blessed with great resources, but the fact is that with 14 million people we sold more unfinished goods with less labour content in them than any other similar number of people in the world. Are we to remain more or less hewers of wood and drawers of water for other countries? I think it is time to stop, look and listen.
What we need in this country is a sound fiscal policy. We need a sound taxation policy. There is very little in this budget that means anything for the municipalities. Canada is a large country, and Canada needs transportation. Canada needs a four-lane highway from

The Budget-Mr. Rowe east to west. Canada is especially adapted to co-operation between the provinces and the dominion. I can remember that election campaign when the billboards were filled with posters depicting the happy family of Liberalism. Never have the provinces in this dominion been more divided than they are today. Unity-how this party carried the olive branch of unity in one hand with the sword of division in the other. In order to keep in power during the last 25 years they were ready to see one province build a highway to the border of the next province.
What have you done? You have robbed the provinces and you have robbed the municipalities. You have taxed the people; you have taken a greater percentage from the people in taxation than any other government since confederation. You have done the least for the provinces of any government since confederation, in the light of our development. We should have had a trans-Canada highway as part of our transportation system.
I can well recall when we were discussing the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway which is now being undertaken. I compliment the government on doing it at long last. The deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway and the development of power on that great system will provide one of the greatest inland water systems in the world. I well remember when I was the leader of the Progressive Conservative party in Ontario in 1936 and suggested that we should do everything we could to bring about the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. I remember some of my hon. friends who sit to your right, and some who are not here today, saying that was childish prattle, that we would never need to deepen the St. Lawrence waterway. They are now the champions of the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. How they have climbed on the bandwagon.
The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) will remember when they said I was talking childish prattle when I suggested that we needed the St. Lawrence development. As the comedian said, that was a few years ago. We now see some of these hon. gentlemen championing great causes to'which they were opposed just a few years ago. My opposition at that time said that we would never need power from the St. Lawrence. They figured that we could get power just like you would buy buns off a shelf. Rather than talk about the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know now why they boast so much about what they are doing. I think the development of power in that district, along with the power that will be developed in the extreme west and the extreme east, will mean a great deal to our future development. I think the transportation of iron ore from Labrador to the inland sections of Ontario, and the transportation in connection with trade and commerce generally through the great St. Lawrence waterway system when it is completed, will be looked upon in the next 25 years as one of the greatest steps in the development of the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A good policy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, a good policy; and your party opposed that policy when we were suggesting it. But, Mr. Speaker, I am also one of those who believe that this country has a great future. I am not at all depressed. All these passing phases in our history are just like shadows at night. The government who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, have been in power for a long time. Now that they are rapidly, conspicuously and awkwardly approaching the twilight of their career, I can see that this country shall go on. It has been very strong to endure even the weaknesses of the policies they have enunciated. They may laugh but had they not had the advantage of fortunate circumstances in

the world the policies they have enunciated or their lack of policies would have caught up with them long before this time.
They are now catching up with them. Just the other day I was wondering how the present government could endure another Easter holiday, in view of the statements that have been made by the Minister of Finance and by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Usually when you see a government starting to fall to pieces the leading lights of that government start to make mistakes, and they make clumsy statements.
I am one of those who believe that we need in Canada many millions more people. I have a keen regard for those men and women who come to this country and who are ready to work. The great Professor Einstein, who died the other day, had a formula involving X, A and B, where X meant one thing, B another and A was work. We need people who are not afraid of work. There is dignity in work, in hard labour.
There are not many members of this house who, one way or another, have not done some hard labour. In fact most members did some hard labour to get here at all, to say nothing of what they have done on the farms or in other places. I think I was happier in the hayfield than I was in election campaigns, as far as work was concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I have great regard for these new Canadians. I have great regard for these men who come from all parts of the world, these Czechoslovaks, these Hungarians, these Polish people, these German people. I have great regard for all these people who have come to this country because they saw here the greatest heritage that has ever been enjoyed by any similar number of people. I feel sympathetic toward the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration with regard to the remark he made. It probably was a slip of the tongue. I always feel sympathetic towards young men. As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as my hon. friend points out, some men are born to greatness, some achieve greatness and some have greatness thrust upon them. But after you have greatness thrust upon you, you sometimes get confused as to whether you were born to it or whether you achieved it.
As I say, I have great Sympathy for the minister. I have made mistakes, and many of them, in the past; most of my friends over on this side have done so also. I would not want to be too critical of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). I realize that this is his first experience in the cabinet. I hope it is not his last. But, Mr. Speaker, I could not help thinking about what happened when he travelled out to the west. He is one who with his colleagues had been so
The Budget-Mr. Rowe zealous to make sure that we dispensed with the word "royal" in the royal mail and with the word "dominion" and everything that had the slightest reference to the British connection.
As he rode out to western Canada in a private car called the "Dominion of Canada" car, I could not help wondering. I was rather proud of the fact that he still used the word "dominion" even though his colleagues did not like that word. They did not like the word "dominion"; they did not like the word "royal". They did not like even the Canadian train to be called the "Royal Canadian". They would rather have it just "Canadian", whether it is any faster or slower. They do not like these things. I was therefore glad that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration still clung to the word "dominion" and had it on the side of his private car. I was glad he had it called the "Dominion of Canada" car.
But despite his zealousness to preserve the name "dominion" I wondered if, when he made his famous speech out there, he had in mind the children of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair). I know the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has lovely children. I saw those little girls. If ever I was charged with anything it would be for kidnapping such beautiful little children. My grandchildren are like them, although they are not any better looking than are the children of the Minister of Fisheries. I am a great lover of children myself; I could adopt any number of them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but if I could get enough children I would buy a private car. I am extremely fond of children. I am glad to see these young cabinet ministers so proud of their children that they think they are better than any other children, or better than children born any place else. There is nothing like local pride. I know my wife often says to me, "Oh, stop talking about your grandchildren; other people also have grandchildren". I know how the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of Fisheries feel about the matter.
After seeing these children I can understand how they could say there are no other children like them. I can appreciate that they are some of Canada's best. But, Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder whether the minister made that statement because the Minister of Trade and Commerce has gone to Australia and is far away. In view of his record since, I think the Hon. C. D. Howe-

Right honourable.

I wonder whether it is because he is away in Australia that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration thought it was fair to take a sideswipe at him and say that if he had been born in Canada he would have made a better minister of trade and commerce. A.	Macdonald, the greatest statesman Canada has ever had, bar none. Next to him is the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and away down the line are some of these satellites. But if Sir John A. As I have gone down the corridors and met my friend the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, whom I have known unparliamentarily for some time as Jack Pickersgill, I have often wondered why he has not been more friendly to me. I thought it was because I was a Conservative but now I find it was because I was born at Hull, Iowa, in the United States. I cannot help that now, at this late date. I cannot help thinking, as a further example of his thoughtless expressions probably arising from his inexperience and exuberance, of another quite prominent debater and wondering whether he forgot him. I have listened to this hon. member often in the house and have come to admire him. I refer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who was not bom in this country either. He must have felt the minister's statement very keenly.
Indeed, Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, one of the first prime ministers of Canada, was not born in Canada either, and he was a prominent Liberal. I believe Hon. George Brown was bom outside of Canada, as was the late Right Hon. D'Arcy McGee. If D'Arcy McGee were here and in his usual form he would describe in a much better way than I can what the minister's statement means so far as making two classes of citizens in the dominion is concerned.
Then I sometimes wonder if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration realizes that

he represents the constituency of Bonavista-Twillingate. I have not been in that section of the country-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Neither has he.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -but he has not been there very much either. I wonder whether he realizes that none of the electors who elected him to parliament were born in Canada. He must have more affection for children than I have, because evidently the only people he really loves in Bonavista-Twillingate are the babies. All those who elected him were born before Newfoundland was a part of Canada at all. I could not help thinking of that song, "Oh, What a Beautiful Baby".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sing it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He may have been a beautiful baby but, baby, look at him now. I wondered whether the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration realized he was not contributing very much to the development of this country by distinguishing these babies as he has. I have imposed on the hospitality of the house for five minutes and there are a lot of other things I should like to say.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But I always feel-
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will not have a more appreciative audience.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will give you until ten
o'clock to score.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the first thing you ever gave me.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is better at taking things away.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There may be other opportunities.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have taken quite a bit from me at different times. I always feel it is not good sportsmanship to impose upon the hospitality of the house when one is given extra time. I think it would be particularly unethical and not showing courtesy to my colleagues on both sides of the house if I were to proceed to say the things I should like to say, because the things I should like to say and should say would not be as unanimously accepted as the extension of time to which you so generously agreed. So I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the time you have given me.
On motion of Mr. Zaplitny the debate was adjourned.
